---
title: "Film Study: All-22, Charting a Game, and Scoring Yourself"
subtitle: "Watch it again the way a coach does, turn a game into rows you can count, and find out how good your Sunday calls really were."
description: "The course's after-the-game routine: why film study answers what live watching can't; getting All-22 coaches film and setting up to study it; the four-pass film-study protocol (freeze at the snap, then the line, the quarterback, the coverage and the skill players, then one 'because' line), worked on a Super Bowl LX strip-sack; game charting with a fixed template and codebook, a skeleton built from nflverse play-by-play, and Super Bowl LX charted end to end from public data; scoring a season's prediction log with hit rate, the Brier score, skill against honest baselines and a calibration plot, in a few lines of Python; resolution versus calibration; and where to keep learning (coaching clinics, the film-breakdown and analytics communities, the Big Data Bowl)."
glossary:
  "Film-study protocol": "A fixed routine for studying each snap on game film: freeze the picture at the snap and check your pre-snap read, then watch the play once for each group (the offensive line, the quarterback, the coverage, the receivers and backs), and finish with one line saying why the play worked or failed. The order runs from what sets the play's clock to what uses it."
  "Game charting": {def: "Recording every snap of a game as one row of the same fixed fields (situation, personnel, formation, motion, the defense's look, what happened after the snap, the result), coded the same way every time, so that a game becomes data you can count, compare and check your predictions against.", aliases: ["Charting"]}
  "Brier score": "The average, over a set of probability forecasts, of the squared gap between the stated probability and what happened (1 if it came true, 0 if not). Lower is better: 0 is perfect, saying 50% every time scores 0.25, and a confident miss costs far more than a timid one. Named for the meteorologist Glenn Brier, who proposed it in 1950."
  "Brier skill score": "One minus the ratio of your Brier score to a reference forecaster's on the same events: 0 means no better than the reference, positive means better, and 1 would be perfect."
  "Proper scoring rule": "A way of scoring probability forecasts whose expected score is best when you state exactly the probability you believe, so it can't be gamed by shading numbers up or down. The Brier score and log loss are proper."
  "Resolution": "How much a forecaster's stated probabilities sort events apart: different numbers on different occasions, with the higher numbers really coming true more often. One of the three parts of the Brier score; it's the part that rewards knowing more, where calibration rewards knowing how sure to be."
  "Calibration": "How closely stated confidences match how often things come true: a well-calibrated forecaster's 70% calls come true about 70% of the time. Shown on a calibration plot (stated confidence against the actual hit rate, with the diagonal as perfect); points below the diagonal mean overconfidence, points above it underconfidence."

```{python}
import os
import re
import tempfile
import textwrap
import logging

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch, FancyArrowPatch, Rectangle, Circle, Patch
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

from gridiron import Play, Player, offense, defense, routes as r, style, draw_marker, show_animation

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
LOOK = "#0f7a55"           # "look here" badges (a darker step of the aqua highlight)
AUTO_TINT = "#ecebe4"      # chart columns filled automatically from play-by-play
FILM_TINT = "#f6ecd2"      # chart columns that only your film can fill
LOG_TINT = "#dcefe6"       # your live log's columns


def pct(x, nd=0):
    """0.613 -> '61%'."""
    return f"{100 * x:.{nd}f}%"


def blank(ax):
    ax.set_axis_off()
    ax.grid(False)


def no_numbers(ax):
    """Remove the painted yard-line numbers (they sit where wide receivers and corners stand)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()


def tag(fld, play, text, at, fs=7.0, ha="center", color=style.INK, bold=False, ec=style.BASELINE, z=21):
    """A boxed label at alignment coordinates (d, w), drawn above the players."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*at))
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, ha=ha, va="center", fontsize=fs, color=color, zorder=z, linespacing=1.12,
                fontweight="bold" if bold else "normal",
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.25", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=ec, lw=0.6))


def scorebug(fld, play, lines, at, fs=6.6, ha="left"):
    """A small dark scorebug box at (d, w)."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*at))
    fld.ax.text(x, y, "\n".join(lines), ha=ha, va="center", fontsize=fs, color="white", zorder=16,
                linespacing=1.25, fontweight="bold",
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.35", fc="#2b2b2b", ec="none"))


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ print stand-ins for animations
def snapshot(play, t, ax, lateral, window, notes=(), trails=True):
    """Everyone where he is at time t, with faint trails of where he has been and the ball in flight."""
    pos = {k: play.position(k, t) for k in play.players}
    moved = [pl.moved(d=float(pos[k][0]), w=float(pos[k][1])) for k, pl in play.players.items()]
    q = Play([m for m in moved if m.side == "off"], [m for m in moved if m.side == "def"],
             los=play.los, ball_y=play.ball_y, to_go=play.to_go)
    q.highlights = dict(play.highlights)
    for n in notes:
        q.note(*n)
    fld = q.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, title=False)
    no_numbers(fld.ax)
    P = lambda d, w: fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d, w))  # noqa: E731
    t0 = play._compile()[1]
    if trails:
        for k, pl in play.players.items():
            if pl.pos in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
                continue
            pts = np.array([play.position(k, tt) for tt in np.linspace(t0, t, 40)])
            if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) < 0.4:
                continue
            xs, ys = P(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])
            col = style.OFFENSE if pl.side == "off" else style.DEFENSE
            ls = "-" if pl.side == "off" else (0, (3, 2))
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=col, lw=1.0, alpha=0.5, ls=ls, zorder=3)
    if t > 0:
        for who, tgt in play.reads:                               # the quarterback's eyes
            (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P(*play.position(who, t)), P(*play.position(tgt, t))
            ax.plot([float(x0), float(x1)], [float(y0), float(y1)], color=style.THIRD, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 2)),
                    zorder=4)
    return fld


def strip(play, times, labels, lateral, window, ncols=2, width_in=6.5):
    """The print version of an animation: one panel per moment, each titled with what to see."""
    n = len(times)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(n / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    h = nrows * (pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]) + 0.36)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width_in, h), squeeze=False)
    for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for ax, t, lab in zip(axes.flat, times, labels):
        snapshot(play, t, ax, lateral, window)
        ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=8.2, color=style.INK, loc="left")
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.5, w_pad=0.4)
    return fig


def animate_or_strip(play, times, labels, lateral, window):
    """Video on the web, a titled frame strip in print."""
    if PDF:
        strip(play, times, labels, lateral, window)
        plt.show()
    else:
        show_animation(play, times=times)


def wash(fld, play, t, keys, reads=False, alpha=0.66, half=()):
    """Fade the whole picture, then redraw only `keys` (with their trails) on top: one pass of the film.
    Players in `half` are redrawn at half strength, as context for the group being watched."""
    ax = fld.ax
    (x0, x1), (y0, y1) = ax.get_xlim(), ax.get_ylim()
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none",
                           alpha=alpha, zorder=12))
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    P = lambda d, w: fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d, w))  # noqa: E731
    t0 = play._compile()[1]
    for k in list(half) + list(keys):
        pl = play.players[k]
        a_ = 0.5 if k in half else 1.0
        pts = np.array([play.position(k, tt) for tt in np.linspace(t0, t, 50)])
        if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) > 0.4:
            xs, ys = P(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])
            col = style.OFFENSE if pl.side == "off" else style.DEFENSE
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=col, lw=1.4, alpha=a_, ls="-" if pl.side == "off" else (0, (3, 2)), zorder=13)
        x, y = P(*play.position(k, t))
        for a in draw_marker(ax, float(x), float(y), pl.side, pl.label, ppy, ring=play.highlights.get(k)):
            a.set_zorder(a.get_zorder() + 10)
            if a_ < 1:
                a.set_alpha(a_)
    if reads:
        for who, tgt in play.reads:
            (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = P(*play.position(who, t)), P(*play.position(tgt, t))
            ax.plot([float(xa), float(xb)], [float(ya), float(yb)], color=style.THIRD, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (4, 2)),
                    zorder=13)


def protect(p, linemen=("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT")):
    """Linemen set back into pass protection."""
    for k in linemen:
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])


from gridiron.play import _interp  # noqa: E402  (keyframe interpolation, used by the trail-technique play below)


class TrailPlay(Play):
    """A Play whose man defenders play trail technique: from their alignment at the snap they settle, within
    about a second, a yard behind and a yard inside their receiver ("on his inside hip, underneath").
    gridiron's own p.man() closes the cushion to almost nothing, which draws the defender on top of the
    receiver and hides him; this keeps both visible, and it's the technique 2-Man actually asks for."""

    def __init__(self, *a, **k):
        super().__init__(*a, **k)
        self.trail = {}

    def trail_man(self, key, target, behind=1.0, inside=1.1, lag=0.15, settle=1.0):
        self.trail[key] = (target, behind, inside, lag, settle)
        self._compiled = None
        return self

    def _compile(self):
        if self._compiled is not None:
            return self._compiled
        kf, t_start, t_end = super()._compile()
        for key, (tgt, behind, inside, lag, settle) in self.trail.items():
            own, rec = kf[key], kf[tgt]
            s0, r0 = _interp(own, 0.0), _interp(rec, 0.0)
            off0 = s0 - r0
            want = np.array([-behind, -np.sign(r0[1]) * inside])          # behind him, toward the ball
            rows = [row for row in own if row[0] < 0]
            for t in np.linspace(0.0, t_end + 0.6, 70):
                f = np.clip(t / settle, 0, 1)
                f = f * f * (3 - 2 * f)                                     # ease in, ease out
                rows.append((t, *(_interp(rec, max(t - lag, 0.0)) + off0 * (1 - f) + want * f)))
            kf[key] = np.array(rows, dtype=float)
        self._compiled = (kf, t_start, t_end)
        return self._compiled
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (data: nflverse play-by-play, FTN charting and participation, 2024–2025)"
#| output: false
from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

PCOLS = ["season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "defteam", "play_type", "down", "ydstogo", "yardline_100",
         "yrdln", "pass", "qb_dropback", "xpass", "week", "qtr", "time", "fixed_drive", "fixed_drive_result",
         "yards_gained", "epa", "success", "sack", "interception", "fumble_lost", "touchdown", "pass_location",
         "run_location", "score_differential", "desc", "rusher_player_name", "receiver_player_name"]
FTN_COLS = ["game_id", "play_id", "starting_hash", "qb_location", "n_offense_backfield", "is_motion", "is_no_huddle",
            "is_play_action", "is_screen_pass", "is_rpo", "n_pass_rushers", "n_blitzers"]
PART_COLS = ["game_id", "play_id", "offense_personnel", "defense_personnel", "defenders_in_box",
             "defense_coverage_type", "defense_man_zone_type", "was_pressure", "time_to_throw"]


def load_season(season):
    """Runs and dropbacks, with FTN charting and participation attached."""
    d = pbp([season], columns=PCOLS)
    d = d[d.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"]) & d.down.notna()].copy()
    d["play_id"] = d.play_id.astype(float)
    f = nfl().load_ftn_charting([season]).to_pandas()
    f = f.rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id", "nflverse_play_id": "play_id"})
    f["play_id"] = f.play_id.astype(float)
    p = nfl().load_participation([season]).to_pandas().rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id"})
    p["play_id"] = p.play_id.astype(float)
    return (d.merge(f[FTN_COLS], on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="left")
             .merge(p[PART_COLS], on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="left"))


def count_pos(s, keys):
    if not isinstance(s, str):
        return np.nan
    c = {k: int(v) for v, k in re.findall(r"(\d+) ([A-Z]+)", s)}
    return sum(c.get(k, 0) for k in keys)


def pers_code(s):
    """FTN-era personnel string ('1 C, 2 G, 1 QB, 1 RB, 2 T, 1 TE, 3 WR') -> '11'."""
    if not isinstance(s, str):
        return "?"
    c = {k: int(v) for v, k in re.findall(r"(\d+) ([A-Z]+)", s)}
    return f"{c.get('RB', 0) + c.get('FB', 0)}{c.get('TE', 0)}"


COV = {"COVER_0": "C0", "COVER_1": "C1", "COVER_2": "C2", "2_MAN": "2M", "COVER_3": "C3", "COVER_4": "C4",
       "COVER_6": "C6", "COVER_9": "C9", "COMBO": "CMB", "BLOWN": "BLN", "PREVENT": "PRV"}
TWO_HIGH = {"C2", "2M", "C4", "C6"}
ONE_HIGH = {"C0", "C1", "C3", "C9"}          # C0 has nobody deep; "not two-high" for the shell call


def chart_codes(d):
    """The public charting, written in the chart sheet's short codes."""
    d = d.copy()
    d["pers"] = d.offense_personnel.map(pers_code)
    nb = d.n_offense_backfield
    d["align"] = d.qb_location.fillna("?") + nb.map(lambda v: "?" if pd.isna(v) else str(int(min(v, 2))))
    d["mot"] = np.where(d.is_motion.fillna(False).astype(bool), "M", "–")
    d["ndb"] = d.defense_personnel.map(lambda s: count_pos(s, ("CB", "FS", "SS", "S", "DB")))
    d["dpers"] = d.ndb.map(lambda v: {4: "base", 5: "nickel", 6: "dime", 7: "quarter"}.get(int(v), "?")
                           if pd.notna(v) else "?")
    d["box"] = d.defenders_in_box.map(lambda v: "?" if pd.isna(v) else str(int(v)))
    d["cv"] = d.defense_coverage_type.map(COV)
    d["rush"] = d.n_pass_rushers
    kind = np.where(d.qb_dropback == 1, "P", "R")
    kind = np.where(d.is_play_action.fillna(False).astype(bool) & (kind == "P"), "PA", kind)
    kind = np.where(d.is_screen_pass.fillna(False).astype(bool), "SCR", kind)
    d["kind"] = kind
    d["is_pass"] = (d.qb_dropback == 1).astype(int)

    def res(row):
        if row.sack == 1:
            return "sk FUM" if row.fumble_lost == 1 else f"sk {int(row.yards_gained):+d}".replace("-", "−")
        if row.interception == 1:
            return "INT"
        if row.fumble_lost == 1:
            return "FUM"
        if row.touchdown == 1:
            return "TD"
        return f"{int(row.yards_gained):+d}".replace("-", "−")
    d["res"] = d.apply(res, axis=1)
    d["hash"] = d.starting_hash.where(d.starting_hash.isin(["L", "M", "R"]), "?")   # FTN writes 0 when unknown
    return d


S24 = load_season(2024)
S25 = load_season(2025)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ Super Bowl LX, both offenses
SB_ID = "2025_22_SEA_NE"
SB = chart_codes(S25[S25.game_id == SB_ID]).sort_values("play_id").reset_index(drop=True)
NE = SB[SB.posteam == "NE"]
SEA = SB[SB.posteam == "SEA"]
NE_DB = NE[NE.qb_dropback == 1]
NE_LAB = NE_DB[NE_DB.cv.isin(TWO_HIGH | ONE_HIGH)]
SBX = dict(
    ne_snaps=len(NE), ne_db=len(NE_DB), ne_pass=float(NE.is_pass.mean()),
    four=int((NE_DB.rush == 4).sum()), five=int((NE_DB.rush >= 5).sum()),
    sacks=int(NE.sack.sum()), sacks4=int(((NE.sack == 1) & (NE.rush == 4)).sum()),
    press=float(NE_DB.was_pressure.fillna(False).astype(float).mean()),
    two=float(NE_LAB.cv.isin(TWO_HIGH).mean()), n_lab=len(NE_LAB),
    man=float((NE_DB.defense_man_zone_type == "MAN_COVERAGE").sum()
              / NE_DB.defense_man_zone_type.isin(["MAN_COVERAGE", "ZONE_COVERAGE"]).sum()),
    sea_snaps=len(SEA), sea_run=float(1 - SEA.is_pass.mean()), sea_uc=float((SEA.qb_location == "U").mean()),
    walker_n=int((SEA.rusher_player_name == "K.Walker").sum()),
    walker_y=int(SEA.loc[SEA.rusher_player_name == "K.Walker", "yards_gained"].sum()),
    ne_succ=float(NE.success.mean()), sea_succ=float(SEA.success.mean()),
)

_R25 = S25[S25.season_type == "REG"]
SBX["ne_reg_pass"] = float(_R25.loc[_R25.posteam == "NE", "qb_dropback"].mean())
SBX["sea_reg_run"] = float(1 - _R25.loc[_R25.posteam == "SEA", "qb_dropback"].mean())

# Seattle's defense against dropbacks in the 2025 regular season, and the league's
REG = S25[(S25.season_type == "REG") & (S25.qb_dropback == 1)].copy()
REG["c"] = REG.defense_coverage_type.map(COV)
REG_LAB = REG[REG.c.isin(TWO_HIGH | ONE_HIGH)]
SEA_REG = REG_LAB[REG_LAB.defteam == "SEA"]
SEASON = dict(sea_two=float(SEA_REG.c.isin(TWO_HIGH).mean()), lg_two=float(REG_LAB.c.isin(TWO_HIGH).mean()),
              sea_four=float((REG[(REG.defteam == "SEA") & (REG.n_pass_rushers > 0)].n_pass_rushers == 4).mean()),
              lg_four=float((REG[REG.n_pass_rushers > 0].n_pass_rushers == 4).mean()),
              sea_press=float(REG.loc[REG.defteam == "SEA", "was_pressure"].fillna(False).astype(float).mean()),
              lg_press=float(REG.was_pressure.fillna(False).astype(float).mean()))


def sea_two_rate(down):
    """Seattle's 2025 regular-season two-high rate on dropbacks, by down (1st, 2nd, 3rd/4th)."""
    dd = SEA_REG.down.clip(upper=3)
    return float(SEA_REG.loc[dd == min(down, 3), "c"].isin(TWO_HIGH).mean())


# The strip-sack: third-and-6, end of the third quarter
SS_ROW = NE[(NE.qtr == 3) & (NE.sack == 1) & (NE.fumble_lost == 1)].iloc[0]

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ the pre-snap model (situation + formation)
def feats(d):
    xp = np.clip(d.xpass.astype(float), 1e-3, 1 - 1e-3)
    nb = d.n_offense_backfield.fillna(1)
    return np.column_stack([np.ones(len(d)), np.log(xp / (1 - xp)), d.qb_location == "S", d.qb_location == "P",
                            nb == 0, nb >= 2]).astype(float)


def fit(X, y, lam=1.0, iters=30):
    """Ridge-penalised logistic regression by Newton's method (numpy only)."""
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(iters):
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-X @ w))
        H = X.T @ (X * (p * (1 - p))[:, None]) + lam * np.eye(X.shape[1])
        w -= np.linalg.solve(H, X.T @ (p - y) + lam * w)
    return w


TR = S24[(S24.season_type == "REG") & S24.xpass.notna()]
W_INFO = fit(feats(TR), TR["pass"].values.astype(float))


def p_info(d):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-feats(d) @ W_INFO))


def conf_of(p, cap=0.9):
    return float(np.clip(np.round(max(p, 1 - p) * 20) / 20, 0.5, cap))


SB["p_rule"] = p_info(SB)
SB["call"] = np.where(SB.p_rule >= 0.5, "P", "R")
SB["conf"] = SB.p_rule.map(conf_of)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ a simulated reader: every Panthers snap of 2025
CAR = S25[(S25.posteam == "CAR") & S25.xpass.notna()].sort_values(["week", "play_id"]).reset_index(drop=True)
CAR["p_info"] = p_info(CAR)
GAMES = list(dict.fromkeys(CAR.game_id))
CAR["g"] = CAR.game_id.map({g: i for i, g in enumerate(GAMES)})
N_GAMES = len(GAMES)
LG = np.log(CAR.p_info / (1 - CAR.p_info)).values
Y = CAR["pass"].values.astype(int)


def simulate(k0, k1, s0, s1, cap0, cap1, seed):
    """A reader who sees what the model sees, through noise, and over- or under-states it.
    k > 1 overstates, k < 1 understates; both settle over the season from (k0, s0, cap0) to (k1, s1, cap1)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    frac = (CAR.g / (N_GAMES - 1)).values
    k, sd = k0 + (k1 - k0) * frac, s0 + (s1 - s0) * frac
    cap = np.where(frac < 0.45, cap0, cap1)
    pr = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(k * LG + rng.normal(0, 1, len(CAR)) * sd)))
    conf = np.clip(np.round(np.maximum(pr, 1 - pr) * 20) / 20, 0.5, cap)
    return np.where(pr >= 0.5, "P", "R"), conf


ME_CALL, ME_CONF = simulate(1.5, 0.95, 0.6, 0.4, 0.95, 0.90, seed=15)
A_CALL, A_CONF = simulate(2.2, 2.2, 0.3, 0.3, 0.99, 0.99, seed=7)
B_CALL, B_CONF = simulate(0.35, 0.35, 0.1, 0.1, 0.85, 0.85, seed=7)


LOGDF = pd.DataFrame({
    "game": CAR.g + 1, "week": CAR.week.astype(int), "opp": CAR.defteam, "down": CAR.down.astype(int),
    "togo": CAR.ydstogo.astype(int), "align": CAR.qb_location.fillna("?") + CAR.n_offense_backfield.map(
        lambda v: "?" if pd.isna(v) else str(int(min(v, 2)))),
    "call": ME_CALL, "conf": ME_CONF,
    "clue": np.where(np.abs(CAR.p_info - CAR.xpass) > 0.10, "align", "sit"),
    "result": np.where(Y == 1, "P", "R")})
HIT = (LOGDF.call == LOGDF.result).values.astype(float)


def brier_of(conf, hit):
    return float(np.mean((np.asarray(conf) - np.asarray(hit)) ** 2))


BASE_P = float(Y.mean())
REF = dict(half=0.25, base=BASE_P * (1 - BASE_P), xpass=float(np.mean((CAR.xpass.values - Y) ** 2)),
           info=float(np.mean((CAR.p_info.values - Y) ** 2)), me=brier_of(ME_CONF, HIT))
FIRST = (CAR.g < 8).values
ME = dict(n=len(CAR), acc=float(HIT.mean()), conf=float(ME_CONF.mean()),
          b1=brier_of(ME_CONF[FIRST], HIT[FIRST]), b2=brier_of(ME_CONF[~FIRST], HIT[~FIRST]),
          a1=float(HIT[FIRST].mean()), a2=float(HIT[~FIRST].mean()),
          c1=float(ME_CONF[FIRST].mean()), c2=float(ME_CONF[~FIRST].mean()),
          xpass_acc=float(((CAR.xpass >= 0.5).astype(int) == Y).mean()),
          info_acc=float(((CAR.p_info >= 0.5).astype(int) == Y).mean()))
DD_RUN = ((CAR.ydstogo <= 3) & (CAR.down != 3)) | ((CAR.down == 1) & (CAR.ydstogo <= 6))
ME["dd_acc"] = float((np.where(DD_RUN, 0, 1) == Y).mean())
_AL = (LOGDF.clue == "align").values
ME["align_me"] = float(HIT[_AL].mean())
ME["align_x"] = float(((CAR.xpass.values[_AL] >= 0.5).astype(int) == Y[_AL]).mean())
ME["always"] = BASE_P


def top_band(conf, hit, lo):
    m = np.asarray(conf) >= lo
    return float(np.asarray(hit)[m].mean()), int(m.sum())


ME["top1"], ME["n_top1"] = top_band(ME_CONF[FIRST], HIT[FIRST], 0.9)
ME["top2"], ME["n_top2"] = top_band(ME_CONF[~FIRST], HIT[~FIRST], 0.9)
ME["mid1"], ME["n_mid1"] = (lambda m: (float(HIT[FIRST][m].mean()), int(m.sum())))(
    (ME_CONF[FIRST] >= 0.7) & (ME_CONF[FIRST] < 0.8))

# Readers A and B for the drill
HIT_A = ((A_CALL == "P") == (Y == 1)).astype(float)
HIT_B = ((B_CALL == "P") == (Y == 1)).astype(float)


def recalibrated(conf, hit):
    """Brier score if every stated value were replaced by its own hit rate (perfect calibration, same calls)."""
    t = pd.DataFrame({"c": conf, "h": hit})
    return brier_of(t.groupby("c").h.transform("mean"), t.h)


AB = dict(a_acc=float(HIT_A.mean()), b_acc=float(HIT_B.mean()), a_b=brier_of(A_CONF, HIT_A),
          b_b=brier_of(B_CONF, HIT_B), a_conf=float(A_CONF.mean()), b_conf=float(B_CONF.mean()),
          a_fix=recalibrated(A_CONF, HIT_A), b_fix=recalibrated(B_CONF, HIT_B),
          a_90=top_band(A_CONF, HIT_A, 0.9), b_top=float(B_CONF.max()))


def murphy(f, o):
    """Brier = reliability − resolution + uncertainty (Murphy 1973), grouping by the distinct forecast values."""
    t = pd.DataFrame({"f": f, "o": o})
    g = t.groupby("f").o.agg(["size", "mean"])
    ob = t.o.mean()
    rel = float((g["size"] * (g.index - g["mean"]) ** 2).sum() / len(t))
    res = float((g["size"] * (g["mean"] - ob) ** 2).sum() / len(t))
    return rel, res, float(ob * (1 - ob))


F_PASS = np.where(ME_CALL == "P", ME_CONF, 1 - ME_CONF)          # the same calls, as a chance of a pass
MUR1 = murphy(F_PASS[FIRST], Y[FIRST])
MUR2 = murphy(F_PASS[~FIRST], Y[~FIRST])

# the season in four stretches (the same split the scoring code prints)
_PART = pd.cut(LOGDF.game, [0, 4, 8, 13, 18], labels=False)
QTR = [brier_of(ME_CONF[_PART == i], HIT[_PART == i]) for i in range(4)]
QTR_ACC = [float(HIT[_PART == i].mean()) for i in range(4)]
QTR_CONF = [float(ME_CONF[_PART == i].mean()) for i in range(4)]


def group_cost(c, h):
    """Expected Brier score per call for a group stated at c that came true a share h of the time."""
    return h * (1 - c) ** 2 + (1 - h) * c ** 2


_A90 = A_CONF >= 0.9
AB["a90_c"], AB["a90_share"] = float(A_CONF[_A90].mean()), float(_A90.mean())
AB["a90_cost"] = group_cost(AB["a90_c"], AB["a_90"][0])
AB["a90_fixcost"] = group_cost(AB["a_90"][0], AB["a_90"][0])
_B_LO = B_CONF <= 0.65
AB["b_lo_c"], AB["b_lo_h"], AB["b_lo_share"] = (float(B_CONF[_B_LO].mean()), float(HIT_B[_B_LO].mean()),
                                                float(_B_LO.mean()))
AB["b_lo_cost"] = group_cost(AB["b_lo_c"], AB["b_lo_h"])

# Seattle's 2025 two-high rate by down, as printed on the scouting card in the second-layer code below
CARD = {d_: round(sea_two_rate(d_), 2) for d_ in (1, 2, 3)}
```

**Super Bowl LX, February 8, 2026.** Seattle sacked Drake Maye `{python} SBX["sacks"]` times, and every one
of them looked the same on television: a pass rusher, a quarterback going down, a replay of the rusher's
celebration. What the broadcast never showed was *why*. On `{python} SBX["sacks4"]` of those
`{python} SBX["sacks"]` sacks, the charting says, Seattle rushed only four players, which means New England
had at least five blockers for four rushers and seven Seahawks were covering. So was it the rush? The
coverage? A quarterback holding the ball? A play call that sent everyone deep on the wrong down? You can't
answer that from the couch on Sunday. You can answer it on Monday, with the coaches' film, a pause button
and a routine, and that's where this chapter starts. It ends with the other thing Monday is for: taking the
season of predictions you've been logging since Part 1 and finding out, with a number, how good they were.

**You'll be able to…**

- Get the All-22 coaches film for a game, set up to study it, and run the four-pass film-study protocol on
  any snap: freeze at the snap and check your read, then watch the line, the quarterback, the coverage and
  the skill players, one pass each, and write one line saying why the play worked or failed.
- Chart a full game with a fixed template and codebook, starting from a skeleton built automatically from
  nflverse play-by-play, and turn the finished chart into tendencies.
- Score a season's prediction log in Python: hit rate, Brier score, skill against honest baselines, and a
  calibration plot, and say what each result tells you to change.
- Tell calibration (knowing how sure to be) apart from resolution (knowing more), and know why a reader needs
  both.
- Know where to keep learning once the course is over: coaching clinics, the film-breakdown and analytics
  communities, and the Big Data Bowl.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
This is the last chapter, and it leans on three earlier ones more than the rest:

- **The live routine** ([Watching Live: The Master Checklist and Anticipation](15-01-watching-live.qmd)):
  the [master pre-snap checklist](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-master-pre-snap-checklist) (situation,
  personnel, formation, motion response, box, shell, leverage, pressure tells, call) and the
  [stated confidence](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stated-confidence) you put on every call, logged in
  the final form of the [prediction log](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-prediction-log).
- **Charting data** ([Tendencies: PROE, Personnel, Motion, and Coverage from Charting Data](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd)):
  [xpass](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-xpass) is the chance of a pass from the situation alone;
  [coverage charting](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-coverage-charting) labels each dropback's coverage
  after the snap, by a person watching film; and every charted label is a judgement with known caveats.
- **The film itself** ([How to Watch a Broadcast Like You Mean It](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
  [coaches film](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-coaches-film) shows every snap from a high sideline angle
  (the [All-22](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-all-22)) and from a high
  [end-zone camera](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-end-zone-camera), with no replays and no on-screen
  graphics (so no scorebug or clock).
:::

## What Sunday can't tell you

Live watching, done well, is prediction. You read the situation and the formation, make a call with a
number on it, and the snap tells you whether the call was right. But the snap only answers the first layer.
It tells you *pass*; it doesn't tell you whether the coverage you called was the coverage that was played,
because the camera was on the quarterback when the safeties turned. It tells you *sack*; it doesn't tell you
whose fault the sack was. It tells you *seven-yard run*; it doesn't tell you whether the run went where it was
designed to go or bounced somewhere else because a block failed. And after a season of logging, a nagging
question: you've been writing "70%" next to calls for months. Do your 70% calls come true seven times in ten?

Those are three different gaps, and this chapter closes each with its own tool:

1. **The film** answers *what happened*, for every player, on every snap. It's the only source that shows all
   22 at once for the whole play.
2. **The chart** turns what happened into rows: one per snap, the same fields every time, so a game can be
   counted instead of remembered. It is also the answer key for your log's second layer.
3. **The score** turns your log into a number that rewards both being right and being honest about how sure
   you were, and a plot that tells you which way to adjust.

Coaches have done the first two for as long as there has been film. In an NFL building, Monday morning belongs
to the last game: every player graded on every snap, the staff deciding what to fix, and the quality control
coaches' tags on every snap feeding the reports the coordinators read
([The Game Plan: A Week Inside an NFL Building](../08-the-chess-match/08-03-game-planning-week.qmd)). The third
is borrowed from weather forecasters, who have been scored this way since 1950. You'll do a fan's version of all
three, with free data, an affordable film subscription and a few dozen lines of Python.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: watching the same play four times"}
Why not just watch the replay carefully once? Because attention is narrower than it feels. In a famous
experiment, viewers asked to count basketball passes in a short video missed a person in a gorilla suit
walking through the middle of the scene; about half of them never saw it.[^gorilla] Football film is that
experiment on every snap: watch the quarterback and you won't see the safety rotate; watch the safety and you
won't see which lineman lost. Coaches solved this long ago by dividing the film: the offensive line coach
watches the line, the secondary coach the secondary. A fan has no staff, so you divide the film by *time*
instead, watching the same snap several times, a different group each time.

What it gives up: time. Four passes on every snap of a game is hours of work, which is why the protocol below
comes with a short version.
:::

## Getting the film

You met coaches film in [How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd): every
snap shown twice, once from the high wide sideline angle that keeps all 22 players in frame, and once from a high
camera behind the end zone. Fans have been able to buy it since 2012. Today it comes with NFL+ Premium, the league's
own subscription: it was part of Premium for the 2026 season, and when the league described the package in 2024 its
archive went back to the 2022 season.[^nflplus] It isn't posted the moment the game ends: the league's help pages say
to expect it 24 to 36 hours after the final whistle, so a Sunday game is ready by Monday night or Tuesday. Packages and
prices change often, so check what's included before you pay.

If you don't have it, you can still do a lot with what's free. The broadcast's own replays include the
[skycam](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-skycam) and end-zone angles on many snaps. Teams post highlight clips,
and several film-breakdown writers post All-22 clips of the plays they analyse (there's a list at the end of the
chapter). None of it is every snap from every angle, which is what charting a whole game needs, but it's plenty
for studying the snaps that mattered. (Which chart columns the broadcast alone can fill is in the codebook below.)

**Setting up.** Three things, side by side if you have the screen for it:

- **The film**, in a player that can pause cleanly on a single frame, step a frame at a time, and slow down to
  half speed. Most of what you'll do is pause on the snap, play a second and a half, and go back. If the
  subscription's own player won't step frames on your device, try it on a computer's browser before you give up on it.
- **The chart**, a spreadsheet with one row per snap ([the template is below](#charting-a-game)), already filled
  with everything the play-by-play knows, so you only type what the film adds.
- **Your live log**, the sheet you kept on Sunday. You'll check it against the film, but you won't change it: it's
  a record of what you knew *before* the snap, and correcting it after watching the film would make your score
  meaningless. Film notes go in their own column, marked as written after the fact.

**Keeping the three lined up.** Coaches film has no scorebug, so it can't tell you which snap you're on; the
play-by-play can. Every row carries the quarter, the clock at the snap, the down and distance and the ball's spot
(`qtr`, `time`, `down`, `ydstogo` and `yrdln` in nflverse), and the film shows the snaps in the order they happened.
Number the snaps in the chart, keep a finger on the down and distance and the yard line (both visible on the field),
and the film, the chart and your log stay on the same row. Your log already has the quarter and clock from Sunday,
which is how the two get joined later.

**Timing a snap.** Several passes below ask you to count seconds from the snap. A phone stopwatch started on the snap
is good to a few tenths, which is enough to tell 2 seconds from 3.5. For better, step frames: video usually runs at 30
or 60 frames a second, so at 30, two and a half seconds is 75 frames.

**Knowing who's who.** Jersey numbers are small in the wide shot. Keep both teams' rosters open, identify players by
where they line up first (the left tackle is the left tackle whatever his number), and confirm a number on the end-zone
angle when it matters.

## The four-pass film protocol

Here is the routine. It's the course's [**film-study protocol**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-film-study-protocol):
a fixed way to study each snap on film, the same way every time. You freeze the picture at the snap and check your
pre-snap read; then you watch the play four times, once for each group (the line, the quarterback, the coverage,
the receivers and backs); then you write one line saying why the play worked or failed. Before any of that,
watch the snap once at full speed, to see the play whole and where the ball went.

Each step uses the angle that shows its group best. The All-22 is the only one with every player in frame, so it's
the angle for the freeze, the coverage and the routes. The end-zone camera looks straight down the line, so it's the
angle for the blocks and for the quarterback's feet and eyes.

```{python}
#| label: fig-protocol-card
#| fig-cap: "The protocol on one card, to keep beside the film. The middle column is the angle of the coaches film to use for each step; the right-hand column is why the step sits where it does: the order runs from what sets the play's clock (the line) to what uses it (the routes and the run)."
items = [
    ("0", "Freeze at the snap",
     "One look at full speed, then pause on the snap. Check the log's pre-snap columns: personnel, formation and "
     "strength, motion and the defense's answer, box, shell, leverage. Write what you missed live.", "All-22",
     "Your read was made here; grade it before you know the result"),
    ("1", "The line (and the front)",
     "First step: forward (run) or back (pass). Run: zone or gap, who pulled, who was left unblocked on purpose, "
     "where the hole opened. Pass: blockers against rushers, the slide, who came free, and when.", "End zone",
     "The line decides how much time everyone else gets"),
    ("2", "The quarterback",
     "Drop and launch point; where his eyes went first; on time or late (count it); the throw he chose against "
     "the one that was there; what pressure did to him. Runs: the mesh and any read.", "End zone,\nthen All-22",
     "Judge what he did with the time pass 1 measured"),
    ("3", "The coverage",
     "Safeties first: their first step, where they finished (middle open or closed). Corners: bail, squat or "
     "trail. Who traveled with motion, who blitzed, who replaced him. Name it, with a confidence.", "All-22",
     "The hardest read; by now you know where the ball went"),
    ("4", "The skill players",
     "The routes as one concept; who was open at the moment the quarterback looked; separation and yards after "
     "the catch. Runs: the back's aim, his cut, yards after contact; blocks by receivers and tight ends.", "All-22",
     "Routes only make sense against the coverage"),
    ("✓", "The 'because' line",
     "One line: why it worked or failed, and whose play it was (either side's call, the line, the quarterback, the "
     "coverage, the skill players). Then fill in the chart row.", "",
     "A snap you can't explain in one line needs another pass"),
]
rows = []
for num, head, body, view, why in items:
    lines_ = textwrap.wrap(body, 56)
    why_ = textwrap.wrap(why, 27)
    rows.append((num, head, lines_, view, why_, max(len(lines_) + 1, len(why_), 2)))
H = sum(r_[5] for r_ in rows) + 0.35 * len(rows) + 3.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 0.19 * H))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0, right=1, top=1, bottom=0)
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_ylim(0, H)
ax.axis("off")
ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((0.8, 0.3), 98.4, H - 0.6, boxstyle="round,pad=0.2,rounding_size=0.8",
                            fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.2))
ax.text(3, H - 1.25, "The four-pass film protocol", fontsize=11.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="center")
ax.text(97, H - 1.25, "one snap, about two minutes", fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="center")
ax.text(9.0, H - 2.55, "WATCH FOR", fontsize=6.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK_2, va="center")
ax.text(60.5, H - 2.55, "ANGLE", fontsize=6.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK_2, va="center")
ax.text(72.0, H - 2.55, "WHY HERE", fontsize=6.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK_2, va="center")
y = H - 3.6
for k, (num, head, lines_, view, why_, h) in enumerate(rows):
    top, bottom = y + 0.55, y - (h - 1) - 0.45
    fc = LOG_TINT if num in ("0", "✓") else "#eef3fb"
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((2.2, bottom), 95.6, top - bottom, boxstyle="round,pad=0.05,rounding_size=0.4",
                                fc=fc, ec="none"))
    ax.scatter([5.3], [y - 0.05], s=150, color=LOOK, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8, zorder=5)
    ax.text(5.3, y - 0.05, num, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.4, color="white", fontweight="bold", zorder=6)
    ax.text(9.0, y, head, fontsize=8.2, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="center")
    for j, ln in enumerate(lines_):
        ax.text(9.0, y - 1 - j, ln, fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK, va="center")
    for j, ln in enumerate(view.split("\n")):
        ax.text(60.5, y - j, ln, fontsize=6.9, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, va="center", fontweight="bold")
    for j, ln in enumerate(why_):
        ax.text(72.0, y - j, ln, fontsize=6.7, color=style.INK_2, va="center", style="italic")
    y -= h + 0.35
plt.show()
```

Each step deserves its reasons.

### Step 0: freeze at the snap

Watch the snap once at full speed first: you want the play as a whole, and the result, before you take it apart.
Then go back to the frame where the ball is snapped and grade your Sunday read. The
pre-snap columns of your log (personnel, alignment, box, shell) were your best guesses from a tight broadcast
shot; the All-22 shows the truth. Was it really two-high, or was the second safety already at eight yards and
creeping? Was the box six or seven? Which way did the defense set its strength, and did a linebacker shift when
the motion went? Write what you missed in a notes column. Don't overwrite the log.

Be honest with yourself here, because you now know how the play turned out. The test for each note is whether it was
*visible at the snap*: "the second safety was at eight yards" is; "it was obviously Cover 3" usually isn't, if the
proof only came after the snap.

This step does two jobs. It grades the *inputs* of your call, which your score can't: a 70% pass call that came
true is a good result, but if you'd miscounted the backfield it was a lucky one. And it trains your live eye. After a
few games you'll find you're consistently wrong about one thing (a safety's depth is a common one, because the
broadcast angle flattens the field), and you'll start correcting for it on Sunday.

### Pass 1: the line

Use the end-zone angle and watch only the ten big men: the five offensive linemen and whoever lines up across from
them, plus any back or tight end who blocks. The first thing to see happens in the first half-second: **did the
line step forward or back?** Coaches say it as "low hats, run; high hats, pass": linemen who fire out low are
blocking a run; linemen who rise and sit back are protecting a pass. Two exceptions. On play-action they fake the
first, so look at how far they go: in the NFL a lineman may be only a yard past the line when a pass is thrown, so a
line that surges and then stops is often a pass. And on an [RPO](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rpo) the line
run-blocks even when the ball is thrown; there the tell is the quarterback and the ball, not the line.

On a run, ask what scheme it was. If every lineman steps the same direction together, it's
[zone blocking](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-blocking) ([Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd)).
If they drive straight ahead in double-teams with no lateral step and no puller, it's
[duo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-duo). If linemen [down-block](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-down-block)
toward the middle while someone [pulls](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pull) across behind them, it's a
[gap scheme](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-gap-scheme) ([Gap and Power Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd)).
Then find the defender nobody blocked. On most runs one is left alone on purpose (the backside end on power, the
[read key](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-read-key) on an option, and often the backside end on inside zone too,
for the quarterback to hold with a fake or for a tight end to cut across and block), and knowing which one tells you
what the play was meant to do. Finally, where did the hole open, and was that where the back ran?

On a pass, count. How many rushed, how many blocked? Which way did the line
[slide](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slide-protection), and did a back or tight end stay in? Then the most useful
habit in pass-protection film: **start counting when the ball is snapped.** If a rusher gets to the quarterback in
under two and a half seconds, the protection lost. If the quarterback still has the ball at three and a half
seconds, something else went wrong first, and pass 2 and pass 3 will tell you what. In between is shared ground: the
protection held long enough for a normal drop, but not forever, so the sack belongs partly to the line and partly to
whatever kept the ball in the quarterback's hand, and passes 2 to 4 decide the split. (Those thresholds are rules of
thumb, not laws; a seven-step drop and a quick game have different clocks, so judge against the drop.) And when the
offense has more blockers than the defense has rushers, ask where the spares went: a center with nobody to block and
a back who helped nobody are part of the sack too.

Why first: the line sets the clock for everyone else. A quarterback with 1.8 seconds and one with 3.5 seconds are
playing different games, and a run's whole design is visible in the line's first two steps.

### Pass 2: the quarterback

Now watch only the quarterback, starting from the end-zone angle. His feet: a three- or five-step drop from the
shotgun (roughly the timing of a five- or seven-step drop from under center, since he starts five yards back), a run
fake, a rollout. His
[launch point](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-launch-point), the spot he throws from. His eyes: where does he look
first, and does he move them? A quarterback working a [progression](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-progression)
turns his head from one receiver to the next in order; one throwing on rhythm hitches once and lets it go at the top
of his drop. Count when the ball comes out, and switch to the All-22 to see what he was looking at.

The question that matters most is a comparison: **the throw he made against the throw that was there.** You'll only
be able to answer it fully after pass 4, but start it here, at the moment he chose. And on runs, the quarterback
still has a job: the [mesh](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mesh) with the back, any read he made (on a zone read,
did he keep or give, and was it right?), and whether his fake sold anything.

Why second: you can only judge what he did with the time you measured in pass 1. Sacks that were the protection's
fault get blamed on quarterbacks every week, and the reverse.

### Pass 3: the coverage

Switch to the All-22 and start at the snap with the **safeties**. Their first step tells you more than anything
else in the secondary: a safety who pedals back and widens is playing a deep half; one who sits flat-footed, reading
the slot receiver, is playing a quarter (and will come downhill if it's a run); one who runs toward the middle is
becoming the single high safety; one who drops down toward the line is rotating into a short zone or taking a man. A second later, ask the question from the coverage chapters: is the middle of the field
[closed](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mofc) (one deep safety in the middle) or
[open](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mofo) (two deep, the middle between them)? That single answer splits the
coverages into families ([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)).

Then the corners: did each one **bail** (turn and run to a deep third), **squat** (sit on a short zone near the
sideline), or **trail** (follow his receiver underneath, with help over the top)? Who traveled with the motion before
the snap? Who blitzed, and who dropped into the spot he left? Defenders looking at the quarterback are usually in
zone; defenders looking at a receiver are usually in man. Then write the coverage family, and a confidence. You never
see the defense's call sheet, so coverage read from film is still an inference, as
[Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd) warned about professional charters'
labels: match coverages turn from zone into man by rule, a cornerback who turned and ran with a receiver might be in
man or simply beaten, and a busted assignment can look like a design.

Why third: coverage is the hardest read on the film and deserves a clean pass with nothing else to look at. And by
now you know where the ball went, so you can tell whether the coverage was beaten, or whether the ball went
somewhere the coverage had already given away.

### Pass 4: the skill players

Last, the receivers, tight ends and backs. On a pass, name the routes as one concept
([Concepts versus Coverages](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd)): smash, flood, mesh, a
four-verticals look. Then go back to the moment pass 2 found, when the quarterback looked or threw, and ask **who was
open then.** "Open" at the moment of the throw is the only kind that matters; a receiver who comes open a second after
the ball is gone wasn't an option. Notice separation, how the receiver beat his man or found the hole in the zone, and
what happened after the catch.

On a run, watch the back: where he aimed, where he cut, how many yards he gained before anyone touched him and how
many after. Then the blockers in space: did a receiver's [crack block](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-crack-block)
seal the edge, did the tight end reach his man?

Why last: routes only make sense against the coverage you identified in pass 3, and "open" only makes sense at the
moment you found in pass 2.

### The "because" line

Finish every snap with one line that says why it worked or failed, and whose play it was. There are six
candidates, and a disciplined charter picks one first and adds a second only if he must:

- **The offense's call.** The play was wrong for the defense it met: a run into an eight-man box, a deep concept
  against a coverage built to stop it. Nobody failed; the play-caller lost the guess.
- **The defense's call.** The mirror image: a pressure or a coverage that beat the protection or the concept by
  design, such as a [simulated pressure](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-simulated-pressure) that left a blocker with
  nobody to block while a defender came free.
- **The line.** A block lost and the play died there.
- **The quarterback.** He had time and an open man, and he did something else.
- **The coverage.** On defense: a rotation took the throw away, or a defender lost his man.
- **The skill players.** A drop, a missed cut, a broken tackle, or a great catch.

"Pass, incomplete, because the boundary safety rotated down and took away the out; QB stayed with it too long" is a
good line. "Bad play" isn't. If you can't write the line, you haven't seen the play yet: watch it again.

### Why four passes, and not more

Why four, and not one per position? Because a fan's eye can hold about one group at a time, and these four groups
answer different questions in an order where each pass gives context to the next (watch the receivers first and
you'll call a receiver "open" who the quarterback never had time to look at). More passes add little: by pass 4
you've seen every player, and what's left is re-watching the moment that matters, which you should do as often as
you need. A snap takes about two minutes this way once you're practised, more at first.

### A full game, in the time you have

About 60 to 65 offensive snaps a side, at two minutes each, is more than four hours for both teams. Few people have that on
a Monday. So run the protocol in layers:

- **Every snap:** step 0 (freeze and check the pre-snap columns) and pass 3 (the coverage), because those are the two
  things the broadcast hid from you and your log's second layer needs.
- **Every third down, red-zone snap, sack, turnover and explosive play**: the full protocol. These are the snaps
  that decided the game, and there are usually 20 to 30 of them. (For an "explosive" use the analysts' version from
  [Expected Points and Success Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd), a run of 10
  yards or more or a pass of 20 or more; staffs vary, and many count runs of 12 or more and passes of 16 or more.)
- **Everything else:** at real speed once, then the chart row.

That's two or three hours for one team's offense against the other's defense, which is a realistic weekly habit.
(Coaches chart the kicking game too, every punt and kickoff; this chapter sticks to the snaps from scrimmage.)

## Film room: one snap, four passes

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seahawks 2025 — Super Bowl LX, the strip-sack"}
**The game:** Seattle beat New England 29–13 in Super Bowl LX on February 8, 2026, at Levi's Stadium in Santa
Clara.[^lx] Late in the third quarter Seattle led only 12–0, all on field goals, and New England had the ball.

**The snap:** third-and-`{python} int(SS_ROW.ydstogo)` at the New England `{python} SS_ROW.yrdln.split()[-1]`,
`{python} SS_ROW.time.lstrip("0")` left in the third quarter. The charting records the Patriots in
`{python} SS_ROW.pers` personnel in the shotgun with one back and motion before the snap; Seattle in its dime package
(six defensive backs) with `{python} SS_ROW.box` in the box; **`{python} int(SS_ROW.rush)` rushers**; and coverage
labelled **2-Man**: [man coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-coverage) underneath with two safeties deep
([2-Man](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-2-man)). Derick Hall sacked Drake Maye, forced a fumble, and Byron
Murphy II recovered at the New England 37. Five snaps later Seattle scored its first touchdown, a 16-yard pass to
AJ Barner, and led 19–0.[^ssfacts]

**Why this snap:** it's the question from the top of the chapter. A four-man rush got the sack; the film decides
whether the rush won it or the coverage did.
:::

The figure is a reconstruction in the same format as the course's other replays: what was charted is exact, and the
rest (who lined up where, the routes, which tackle Hall beat and how long it took) is a typical picture of that call,
drawn to show what each pass of the protocol looks at. On the real film, you'd check every one of those details
yourself.

```{python}
#| label: fig-strip-sack
#| fig-cap: "The strip-sack, third-and-6 (a reconstruction, simulated in Big Data Bowl format). Charted facts: 11 personnel in the shotgun with one back and motion; Seattle's dime (six defensive backs), six in the box; four rushers; 2-Man (man coverage underneath, two safeties deep); a sack by Derick Hall (58, ringed), who forced a fumble. Illustrative: the alignments, the motion (here the tight end, Y, across to the left wing, with his defender, D, following him), the routes, the protection, and the time Hall took. What to notice: in the second panel every receiver has a defender a yard behind him and a yard inside, two safeties sit deep, and the middle linebacker (M) is free because the back stayed in; in the third the left tackle is still riding Hall wide as the quarterback climbs; in the fourth Hall has come back under the tackle to the quarterback."
def strip_sack():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    off = [p_.moved(w=1.5) if p_.key == "RB" else p_.moved(w=-18.5) if p_.key == "X" else p_ for p_ in off]
    dfn = [Player("HALL", "OLB", "def", 1.0, -7.4, label="58"), Player("DT", "DT", "def", 1.0, -1.0),
           Player("DE", "DE", "def", 1.0, 2.4), Player("OLB", "OLB", "def", 1.0, 6.0),
           Player("M", "ILB", "def", 5.0, 0.6, label="M"),
           Player("LCB", "CB", "def", 1.6, -17.6, label="CB"), Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 1.6, 14.2, label="CB"),
           Player("NB", "NB", "def", 3.4, -8.6), Player("DM", "DB", "def", 2.4, 8.2),
           Player("FS", "FS", "def", 12.5, -11.0), Player("SS", "SS", "def", 12.5, 9.0)]
    p = TrailPlay(off, dfn, los=54, to_go=6, ball_y="right")
    p.highlight("HALL")
    # the tight end motions across behind the line (well clear of the linemen) to a wing on the left; his man,
    # D, travels with him at linebacker depth and arrives at the same moment
    y_pts = [(-1.5, -5.0), (-1.5, -13.0), (0.5, -14.6)]                 # offsets from Y's spot (-1.5, 9.0)
    p.motion("Y", pts=y_pts, speed=5.0)
    y_len = float(np.hypot(1.5, 5.0) + 8.0 + np.hypot(2.0, 1.6))
    d_pts = [(0.4, -4.0), (0.4, -12.0), (0.6, -13.0)]                   # offsets from D's spot (2.4, 8.2)
    d_len = float(np.hypot(0.4, 4.0) + 8.0 + np.hypot(0.2, 1.0))
    p.motion("DM", pts=d_pts, speed=5.0 * d_len / y_len)
    for d_, rcv in (("LCB", "X"), ("NB", "H"), ("DM", "Y"), ("RCB", "Z")):
        p.trail_man(d_, rcv)                                             # trail technique: inside hip, underneath
    # offense: six block four. C and LG double the tackle, RG and RT take the right side one-on-one, the back
    # checks the A gap for a blitz and stays to help inside; the LT has Hall alone and rides him wide
    p.block("C", pts=[(-0.7, -0.3)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(-0.7, -0.1)])
    p.block("RG", pts=[(-0.9, 0.4)]); p.block("RT", pts=[(-1.2, 1.4)], speed=1.6)
    p.block("RB", pts=[(1.6, -1.9), (2.4, -2.5)], speed=2.4)
    p.block("LT", pts=[(-1.8, -1.2), (-3.7, -2.0), (-5.2, -2.0)], speed=1.7)
    # routes: a high-low on the left (H out at the sticks, Y in the flat under him), X clears deep, Z digs
    p.route("X", r.go(19)); p.route("H", r.out(7, 4)); p.route("Y", r.flat(2.0, 6.0), side=-1)
    p.route("Z", r.dig(12, 7))
    p.dropback(2.0)
    p.path("QB", [(1.0, -0.2)], speed=2.0, delay=1.4)                   # hitches up into the pocket
    p.read("Z")
    # defense: four rush, three of them held; Hall arcs past the launch point, then comes back under the tackle
    p.rush("DT", pts=[(-1.4, 0.1)], speed=0.9); p.rush("DE", pts=[(-1.4, 0.1)], speed=1.0)
    p.rush("OLB", pts=[(-2.0, -0.4)], speed=1.2)
    p.rush("HALL", pts=[(-3.2, -0.8), (-6.6, -0.4), (-8.6, 2.4), (-7.4, 6.2)], speed=4.3)
    p.drop("M", (4.5, -0.4), speed=2.0)                                  # the low hole, eyes on the quarterback
    p.drop("FS", (19.0, -14.0), speed=3.5); p.drop("SS", (19.0, 10.0), speed=3.5)
    return p


SSP = strip_sack()
T_SACK = 3.3
LAT_SS, WIN_SS = (-24, 21), (-10.5, 21.5)
animate_or_strip(SSP, [0.0, 1.5, 2.7, T_SACK],
                 ["Snap · Y motioned left; D went with him", "+1.5 s · two deep, four in man, M free",
                  "+2.7 s · QB climbs; the LT rides 58 wide", f"+{T_SACK} s · 58 comes back under: strip-sack"],
                 lateral=LAT_SS, window=WIN_SS)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-four-passes
#| fig-cap: "The same snap at 2.7 seconds, watched four times. Each panel fades everyone except the group that pass watches, with the paths they have run so far. Pass 1, the line: four rushers against five linemen and the back; the center and left guard double the tackle, the right side is one-on-one and holding, the back is helping inside, and Hall (58, ringed) has run wide and deep around the left tackle, who is still on him. Pass 2, the quarterback: a short drop, eyes to the right (the green dashed line), then a hitch up into the pocket. Pass 3, the coverage: both safeties in deep halves, the four man defenders a yard behind and inside their receivers (trail technique), and the middle linebacker (M) sitting in the short middle because the back stayed in to block. Pass 4, the skill players: four routes, each with a defender attached (drawn at half strength) and a safety above. A reconstruction, as in the previous figure."
T4 = 2.7
MAN_D = ["LCB", "NB", "DM", "RCB"]
PASSES = [
    ("Pass 1 · the line: 4 rushers, 6 blockers", ["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "RB", "HALL", "DT", "DE", "OLB"], False,
     [("C + LG double the T;\nthe back helps inside", (-8.2, 12.5))], ()),
    ("Pass 2 · the QB: eyes right, hitch, no throw", ["QB"], True, [("2.7 s: still holding it", (-9.0, 11.5))], ()),
    ("Pass 3 · coverage: two deep, five under", MAN_D + ["M", "FS", "SS"], False,
     [("deep half", (15.6, -11.0)), ("deep half", (15.6, 10.0))], ()),
    ("Pass 4 · receivers: anyone open?", ["X", "H", "Y", "Z"], False, [("a defender on every route", (-9.0, 11.5))],
     MAN_D),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.5, 2 * (3.25 * (WIN_SS[1] - WIN_SS[0]) / (LAT_SS[1] - LAT_SS[0]) + 0.36)))
for ax, (title, keys, eyes, tags_, half_) in zip(axes.flat, PASSES):
    fld = snapshot(SSP, T4, ax, LAT_SS, WIN_SS)
    wash(fld, SSP, T4, keys, reads=eyes, half=half_)
    for txt, at in tags_:
        tag(fld, SSP, txt, at, fs=6.0)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.0, color=style.INK, loc="left")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.5, w_pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

Now run the protocol on it, the way you would on the real film.

**Step 0, the freeze.** Third-and-6 near midfield, down 12, sixteen seconds left in the third quarter: a pass, near
certain. The
offense is in 11 personnel in the shotgun; the defense in dime with six in the box and two safeties at about 12
yards. The motion is the useful clue: when the tight end crossed the formation, his defender went *with* him. That's
the [man/zone indicator](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-zone-indicator) from
[Motion and Shifts](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd) voting man. A vote, not a verdict:
Macdonald's defenses disguise heavily and play plenty of match coverage
([Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd)), in which a
defender can travel with a receiver too; and the other answer to watch for is a *bump*, the defenders sliding over a man each, which says zone or match. The two deep
safeties say two-high. Put them together and the pre-snap read is 2-Man or a disguised rotation; on third-and-6 2-Man
is a common answer, because it puts a defender on every receiver short of the sticks and two safeties over the top of
them.

**Pass 1, the line.** Four rushers against six blockers (five linemen and the back). Ask where the two spares went:
here the center and left guard double the tackle, and the back checks the gap in front of him for a blitzing
linebacker, finds none, and stays to help inside. The right side holds one-on-one. That leaves the left tackle alone
on Hall, which is normal: a tackle is expected to handle an edge rusher by himself for a few seconds. He does, riding
Hall wide and deep past the quarterback's launch point; the problem is that Maye climbs, and Hall comes back under. Count
from the snap: in the reconstruction Hall arrives at about `{python} T_SACK` seconds, in the shared zone between 2.5
and 3.5, where the line held long enough for the drop and the rest of the answer is in passes 2 to 4. The charting
doesn't record that time; on the real film it's the first thing you'd measure.

**Pass 2, the quarterback.** Maye takes his drop, looks right, hitches up into the pocket and still doesn't throw.
That's a quarterback with time and no answer, or one who missed an answer. Which, pass 4 will say.

**Pass 3, the coverage.** Both safeties pedal back and widen into deep halves. Underneath, every receiver has a
defender a yard behind him and a yard inside, in [trail technique](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-trail-technique),
so anything short and inside is contested and anything deep has a safety coming. The middle linebacker has the back,
and when the back stays in to block, he has a choice his coach gave him: add himself to the rush, or sit in the short
middle as an extra defender. Here he sits, taking away the throw a quarterback looks for against man (the crossing
route underneath) and, just as important, watching Maye. 2-Man's great weakness is the quarterback scramble: every man
defender has his back to the quarterback, so against a mobile one the linebacker in the low hole and the rushers'
lanes (who keeps him from escaping outside) are part of the coverage. Seven defenders in coverage against four
receivers is the whole idea of rushing four: the rush doesn't have to win quickly, because the coverage is designed
to hold out.

**Pass 4, the skill players.** Against 2-Man, receivers need to win on their own: the route that beats it is the one
that gets *away* from a trailing defender toward the sideline or back toward the quarterback, before the safety
arrives. The drawn concept tries exactly that on the left, an out at the sticks over a flat underneath, with a dig on
the right as the backside throw. At the moment Maye hitched, nobody had won. That's the question to answer on the real
film, frame by frame: was there a window at 2.5 seconds he passed up?

**The "because" line.** In this version: *Sack because of the coverage: 2-Man took away everything inside and short of
the sticks, the protection held for a normal drop, and the four-man rush won late, at 3.3 seconds, when the
quarterback climbed into the edge rusher's second move.* If on the real film Hall had arrived in two seconds, it
would read *because the left tackle lost*, and if a receiver had been open at 2.5 seconds, *because the quarterback
held it*. Same play in the box score, three different lessons. That's what the film is for.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"A sack is a pass-protection failure." Often it isn't. A sack is credited to the rusher who gets there, and the
offensive line usually takes the blame, but a sack is the end of a chain: protection, quarterback, coverage, routes. A
defense that rushes four and covers with seven is betting that its coverage will hold long enough for four rushers to
win *eventually*, and when that bet pays off it's a coverage sack. In Super Bowl LX Seattle rushed four on
`{python} SBX["four"]` of New England's `{python} SBX["ne_db"]` dropbacks and got `{python} SBX["sacks4"]` of its
`{python} SBX["sacks"]` sacks that way. You can't tell from the box score which of those were the line's fault and
which were the coverage's. The film can. (And against a mobile quarterback the bet has a second half: the four
rushers must keep their lanes, so the quarterback can't escape the pocket while the coverage holds.)
:::

## Charting a game

The film tells you what happened on one snap. To learn what a team *does*, you need every snap in the same form, and
that's charting. [**Game charting**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-game-charting) means recording every snap of a
game as one row of the same fixed fields (situation, personnel, formation, motion, the defense's look, what happened
after the snap, the result), coded the same way every time, so a game becomes data you can count. Everyone calls it
[charting](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-charting) for short.

You've been using other people's charting since Part 13. When the participation file says a snap was Cover 6 against
11 personnel, somebody watched that snap and wrote those codes. NFL staffs do it too: their quality control coaches
tag every snap of every opponent, and the tags become the tendency report
([The Game Plan](../08-the-chess-match/08-03-game-planning-week.qmd)). Charting your own game puts you in that chair.

**Why chart, when FTN and nflverse already do?** Three reasons.

1. **Timing.** The public charting doesn't all arrive at once. The play-by-play for a game is usually available within
   hours; FTN's charting (alignment, motion, play-action, rushers) arrives game by game during the season; but
   personnel and coverage labels, in the participation file, arrive only after the season ends, around
   February.[^timing] If you want to know what coverage Seattle played against 12 personnel in *this* season, the public
   data can't tell you until the season is over. Your chart can tell you tonight.
2. **What nobody publishes.** The public files don't record the pre-snap shell (only the coverage after the snap), the
   corners' leverage, the formation's strength, which way the run went relative to that strength, the run scheme, the
   pass concept, the routes of receivers who weren't targeted, or who lost the block on a sack. Those are exactly the
   fields that make a tendency useful, and exactly what step 0 and the four passes record.
3. **The answer key.** Your live log's second layer (the coverage family, the rush, the direction of the run) needs
   something to be scored against. On a 2026 game, until the participation file arrives, your chart is the only answer
   key there is.

### The charting sheet

Here is the template. One row per snap, in seven blocks of columns:

```{python}
#| label: fig-chart-sheet
#| fig-cap: "The charting sheet, with New England's first eight snaps of Super Bowl LX filled in from public data. The sheet is one long row per snap, printed here in two tiers that share the snap number (#). Grey blocks fill themselves from the play-by-play. The blue block (the offense before the snap), the peach block (the defense before the snap) and the lavender block (after the snap) are what you chart from film, filled here from FTN's charting and the participation file where those record the field. Cream-shaded cells are fields no public source records (formation, strength, the pre-snap shell, the corners, the rotation, the play concept, the 'because' line), which only your own film can fill. The green block is your live log, filled here with calls made by rule from the pre-snap columns (as in Watching Live), standing in for yours: a run-or-pass call and its confidence, then a second-layer call (l2) on whether Seattle would play two-high or one-high and its confidence (l2conf), made from Seattle's 2025 rate for the down. Every column is decoded in the codebook below."
SHEET = NE[NE.fixed_drive == NE.fixed_drive.min()].copy()
SHEET["l2conf"] = SHEET.down.map(lambda d_: conf_of(sea_two_rate(int(d_)), cap=0.9))
SHEET["l2"] = SHEET.down.map(lambda d_: "2-hi" if sea_two_rate(int(d_)) >= 0.5 else "1-hi")
SHEET["call"] = SB.set_index("play_id").loc[SHEET.play_id, "call"].values
SHEET["conf"] = SB.set_index("play_id").loc[SHEET.play_id, "conf"].values
SHEET = SHEET.reset_index(drop=True)


def dd(row, i=None):
    return f"{int(row['down'])}&{int(row['ydstogo'])}"


T1 = [("#", 3.0, "auto", lambda r_, i: str(i + 1)), ("qtr clock", 7.0, "auto", lambda r_, i: f"Q{int(r_['qtr'])} {r_['time']}"),
      ("dn&to", 5.2, "auto", dd), ("ball on", 6.4, "auto", lambda r_, i: r_["yrdln"]),
      ("hash", 4.0, "auto", lambda r_, i: r_["hash"]),
      ("pers", 4.2, "off", lambda r_, i: r_["pers"]), ("align", 4.4, "off", lambda r_, i: r_["align"]),
      ("form", 5.0, "film", None), ("str", 3.6, "film", None), ("mot", 3.6, "off", lambda r_, i: r_["mot"]),
      ("dpers", 6.4, "def", lambda r_, i: r_["dpers"]), ("box", 3.6, "def", lambda r_, i: r_["box"]),
      ("shell", 4.4, "film", None), ("CB", 3.6, "film", None)]
T2 = [("#", 3.0, "auto", lambda r_, i: str(i + 1)),
      ("rush", 4.0, "post", lambda r_, i: "–" if pd.isna(r_["rush"]) or r_["qb_dropback"] != 1 else str(int(r_["rush"]))),
      ("cov", 4.0, "post", lambda r_, i: r_["cv"] if isinstance(r_["cv"], str) else "–"), ("rot", 3.6, "film", None),
      ("play", 4.4, "auto", lambda r_, i: r_["kind"]), ("concept", 6.2, "film", None),
      ("dir", 3.4, "auto", lambda r_, i: {"left": "L", "middle": "M", "right": "R"}.get(
          r_["pass_location"] if r_["qb_dropback"] == 1 else r_["run_location"], "–")),
      ("yds", 4.6, "auto", lambda r_, i: r_["res"]), ("succ", 3.8, "auto", lambda r_, i: "✓" if r_["success"] == 1 else "✗"),
      ("call", 3.6, "log", lambda r_, i: r_["call"]), ("conf", 4.0, "log", lambda r_, i: f"{r_['conf']:.2f}".lstrip("0")),
      ("l2", 4.0, "log", lambda r_, i: r_["l2"]), ("l2conf", 4.8, "log", lambda r_, i: f"{r_['l2conf']:.2f}".lstrip("0")),
      ("because", 10.0, "film", None)]
FILL = {"auto": AUTO_TINT, "off": style.OFFENSE_TINT, "def": style.DEFENSE_TINT, "post": "#efe3f4", "log": LOG_TINT,
        "film": FILM_TINT}
GROUPS1 = [("FROM PLAY-BY-PLAY", 0, 5, "auto"), ("OFFENSE BEFORE THE SNAP", 5, 10, "off"),
           ("DEFENSE BEFORE THE SNAP", 10, 14, "def")]
GROUPS2 = [("AFTER THE SNAP", 1, 4, "post"), ("THE PLAY AND RESULT", 4, 9, "auto"), ("YOUR LIVE LOG", 9, 13, "log"),
           ("FILM", 13, 14, "film")]
nr = len(SHEET)
RH, HH, GH = 1.0, 1.15, 1.0
tier_h = GH + HH + RH * nr
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.5, 2 * 0.2 * (tier_h + 0.6)))
for ax, cols, groups in ((axes[0], T1, GROUPS1), (axes[1], T2, GROUPS2)):
    blank(ax)
    Wt = sum(w for _, w, _, _ in cols)
    ax.set_xlim(0, Wt)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.3, tier_h + 0.3)
    xs = np.cumsum([0] + [w for _, w, _, _ in cols])
    for name, a, b, kind in groups:
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((xs[a], tier_h - GH), xs[b] - xs[a], GH, fc=FILL[kind], ec="white", lw=1.2))
        ax.text((xs[a] + xs[b]) / 2, tier_h - GH / 2, name, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=5.6,
                fontweight="bold", color=style.INK_2)
    yh = tier_h - GH - HH
    for j, (name, w, kind, fn) in enumerate(cols):
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((xs[j], yh), w, HH, fc=FILL[kind], ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))
        ax.text(xs[j] + w / 2, yh + HH / 2, name, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=5.8, fontweight="bold",
                color=style.INK)
        for i_, (_, row) in enumerate(SHEET.iterrows()):
            yy = yh - (i_ + 1) * RH
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((xs[j], yy), w, RH, fc=FILM_TINT if fn is None else "white", ec=style.GRID,
                                   lw=0.6))
            if fn is not None:
                ax.text(xs[j] + w / 2, yy + RH / 2, fn(row, i_), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=5.8,
                        color=style.INK)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.005, right=0.995, top=0.995, bottom=0.005, hspace=0.18)
plt.show()
```

And here is the codebook that goes with it. The codes matter less than the rule behind them: **decide them before you
start, write them on the sheet, and use them the same way on every snap.** A chart in which "Cover 3" meant one thing in
the first quarter and another in the fourth can't be counted.

| Column | Codes | The rule | TV? |
|:-----|:------------------|:-----------------------|:--:|
| `qtr clock` | Q1 15:00 | Quarter and game clock at the snap | ✓ |
| `dn&to` | 3&6 | Down and yards to go | ✓ |
| `ball on` | NE 44 | The ball's spot (the side of the field, then the yard line) | ✓ |
| `hash` | L, M, R | Where the ball was spotted: left hash, middle, right hash | ✓ |
| `pers` | 11, 12, 21, 13, 10, 22 … | Backs, then tight ends; count as they run on | ✓ |
| `align` | U, S or P plus the number of backs: U1, S0, P1 | Where the quarterback stands, how many in the backfield | ✓ |
| `form` | 2x2, 3x1, bunch, empty 3x2, I, offset I … | Pick one name per look and reuse it | some |
| `str` | L, R | The strong side, by one rule you write at the top of the sheet (tight end, receivers, or field) | some |
| `mot` | –, M (motion), S (shift), J (still moving at the snap) | What moved, and when | ✓ |
| `dpers` | base, nickel, dime | Count the defensive backs | some |
| `box` | a number | Defenders in the [box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box-count) (from just outside the end men on the line, about 5 to 7 yards deep), counted at the snap, after any motion | some |
| `shell` | 0, 1, 2 | Deep safeties at the snap (before any rotation) | rarely |
| `CB` | P or O, plus i or o | Press or off; inside or outside leverage | rarely |
| `rush` | a number | Rushers after the snap | some |
| `cov` | C0, C1, C2, 2M, C3, C4, C6, C9, `?` | The coverage played after the snap | rarely |
| `rot` | –, B, F; add `*` if late (`B*`) | Rotation: none, to the boundary, to the field; the star marks one that started at or after the snap | rarely |
| `play` | R, P, PA, SCR, RPO | Run, dropback, play-action, screen, run-pass option; a scramble is a dropback (P), a designed quarterback run is a run (R) | ✓ |
| `concept` | IZ, OZ, PWR, CTR, DUO, TRAP, TOSS, ZR (zone read), QB (designed QB run); smash, flood, mesh, stick … | The run scheme or pass concept, in the course's names | some |
| `dir` | L, M, R | Where the run hit or the pass went | ✓ |
| `yds` | +7, −3, sk −7, INT, FUM, TD | The result: yards, a sack, a turnover or a score | ✓ |
| `succ` | ✓ or ✗ | A successful play: positive EPA, nflverse's `success` flag ([Expected Points and Success Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd)) | ✓ |
| `call`, `conf` | P or R; 0.50 to 0.90 | Your live log: the run-or-pass call and its stated confidence | ✓ |
| `l2`, `l2conf` | 2-hi, 1-hi, zone, man, 5+, left …; 0.50 to 0.90 | Your live log's second-layer call and *its* confidence (how sure you were of that call, as for `conf`) | ✓ |
| `because` | free text | One line from the protocol: whose play it was | |

: The codebook for the charting sheet. `?` is always allowed and is better than a guess. The last column says whether a careful viewer can usually fill the field from the broadcast alone: ✓ yes, "some" on most snaps, "rarely" only when a replay happens to show it. {#tbl-codebook}

Three rules keep a chart honest:

- **`?` is a code.** If the broadcast cut away, or you can't tell Cover 1 from Cover 3 on a late rotation, write `?`.
  A guessed label looks exactly like a real one in the totals and quietly poisons them.
- **Code what you see, not what you expect.** Charting a team you've studied, you'll be tempted to write its favourite
  coverage before you've watched the safeties. That's how a tendency becomes a self-fulfilling one in your chart.
- **Never edit the live log.** The chart is what happened; the log is what you knew before it happened. Keep them in
  separate columns and score one against the other.

### The skeleton: let the play-by-play do the typing

A third of the sheet is already known before you press play: the snap order, the clock, down and distance, the ball's
spot, the result. nflverse publishes all of it within hours of each game, so the sensible way to start a chart is
to build the skeleton in code and spend your film time only on what the film adds. This function does it for any game
in any season nflverse covers:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from gridiron.data import pbp

FILM_COLUMNS = ["pers", "align", "form", "str", "mot", "dpers", "box", "shell", "CB",
                "rush", "cov", "rot", "concept", "because", "notes"]


def chart_skeleton(game_id, team):
    """One row per snap of `team`'s offense, with the play-by-play columns filled and the film columns empty."""
    season = int(game_id[:4])
    d = pbp([season])
    d = d[(d.game_id == game_id) & (d.posteam == team) & d.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"])
          & d.down.notna()]               # a two-point try has no down; it isn't a charted snap
    sheet = pd.DataFrame({
        "play_id": d.play_id.astype(int), "qtr": d.qtr.astype(int), "clock": d.time,
        "down": d.down.astype(int), "togo": d.ydstogo.astype(int), "ball_on": d.yrdln,
        "play": np.where(d.qb_dropback == 1, "P", "R"),        # scrambles and sacks are dropbacks
        "dir": d.pass_location.fillna(d.run_location).str[0].str.upper(),
        "yds": d.yards_gained.astype(int), "success": d.success.astype(int), "epa": d.epa.round(2)})
    for c in FILM_COLUMNS:
        sheet[c] = ""                     # yours to fill from the film
    return sheet.reset_index(drop=True)


sheet = chart_skeleton("2025_22_SEA_NE", "NE")          # Super Bowl LX, New England's offense
print(f"{len(sheet)} snaps; first five of the play-by-play half:")
print(sheet.iloc[:5, :11].to_string(index=False))
```

The skeleton *is* the blank template: save it with `sheet.to_csv("sb60_ne.csv", index=False)`, open it in a
spreadsheet next to the film, and the empty columns, in the codebook's order, are the ones to fill. (Penalties that
wipe out a snap, kneels and spikes aren't in it; add a row by hand if a wiped-out snap told you something.) For a
current-season game, the same call gives you the skeleton within hours of the game, weeks or months before the public
coverage labels exist.

### Is your chart any good?

Professional charters disagree with each other, and you'll disagree with yourself. The cheap test is to chart one
quarter twice, a week apart, without looking at the first attempt, and compare. For each film column, count how often
the two attempts agree. Personnel and the box should agree almost every time; if they don't, your definition is fuzzy
