(where exactly does "the box" end?). Coverage will agree less often, and that's normal: it's the hardest column, and
the place to use `?` more freely. If you want a single number that allows for agreement by chance, Cohen's kappa is the
standard one.[^kappa] You don't need it to learn something: the columns where you disagree with yourself are the ones
to stop trusting in your totals, and the ones to practise.

## Film room: a whole game, charted

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seahawks 2025 — Super Bowl LX, charted end to end"}
**The game:** Seahawks 29, Patriots 13, Super Bowl LX. In 2025 Seattle's head coach was Mike Macdonald, its offensive
coordinator Klint Kubiak and its defensive coordinator Aden Durde; New England's offensive coordinator was Josh
McDaniels.[^lx2] [The Game Plan](../08-the-chess-match/08-03-game-planning-week.qmd) rebuilt, from public charting, the
tendency report New England's staff might have read about Seattle's defense before this game. This is the game itself.

**The chart:** every one of the game's `{python} SBX["ne_snaps"] + SBX["sea_snaps"]` runs and dropbacks, both offenses,
in the sheet's codes, filled from the public charting (play-by-play, FTN and the participation file, which covers
the playoffs).[^sbdata] The film-only columns are left empty: they're yours.

**What to notice:** how much of the game's story is visible in the rows, and how much isn't.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-game-board
#| fig-cap: "Super Bowl LX on one page: every run and dropback, one cell per snap, one row per drive, New England's offense on top and Seattle's below. Blue cells are dropbacks (including sacks and scrambles), amber cells runs; a dark outline marks a successful play (one with positive EPA: it left the offense better placed to score than before the snap). For dropbacks the top line gives the number of rushers and the charted coverage (2M = 2-Man, C6 = Cover 6, and so on; '–' where none was charted); for runs it says 'run'. The bottom line is the result: yards, a sack, an interception (INT), a lost fumble (FUM) or a touchdown (TD). The right-hand label is how the drive ended. What to notice: the Patriots' first nine drives, none longer than eight snaps, eight ending in punts and the ninth in the strip-sack, against a defense rushing four on almost every dropback and playing two-deep behind it; and Seattle's offense, steady rather than explosive, turning four of its first seven drives into field goals. Source: nflverse play-by-play, FTN charting and participation, game 2025_22_SEA_NE."
RES_TXT = {"Punt": "punt", "Field goal": "FG", "Touchdown": "TD", "Turnover": "turnover", "Opp touchdown": "pick-six",
           "End of half": "end", "Missed field goal": "missed FG", "Turnover on downs": "downs"}


def board(ax, T, title):
    drives = list(dict.fromkeys(T.fixed_drive))
    nmax = 10
    CW, RH_ = 1.0, 1.0
    LW_ = 3.7
    ax.set_xlim(-LW_, nmax * CW + 2.2)
    ax.set_ylim(len(drives) + 0.15, -1.25)
    blank(ax)
    ax.text(-LW_, -0.75, title, fontsize=8.2, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="center")
    for i_, dv in enumerate(drives):
        Dd = T[T.fixed_drive == dv]
        r0 = Dd.iloc[0]
        ax.text(-0.15, i_ + 0.5, f"Q{int(r0.qtr)} {r0.time.lstrip('0')} · {r0.yrdln}", ha="right", va="center",
                fontsize=5.6, color=style.INK_2)
        for j, (_, row) in enumerate(Dd.iterrows()):
            x0 = j * CW
            is_p = row.qb_dropback == 1
            fc = style.OFFENSE_TINT if is_p else "#fbe8b8"
            ok = row.success == 1
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0 + 0.04, i_ + 0.06), CW - 0.08, RH_ - 0.12, fc=fc,
                                   ec=style.INK if ok else "white", lw=1.0 if ok else 0.4))
            if is_p:
                ru = "–" if pd.isna(row.rush) else str(int(row.rush))
                cv = row.cv if isinstance(row.cv, str) else "–"
                top = f"{ru}·{cv}"
            else:
                top = "run"
            ax.text(x0 + CW / 2, i_ + 0.34, top, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=4.9, color=style.INK)
            bad = row.res.startswith("sk") or row.res in ("INT", "FUM")
            ax.text(x0 + CW / 2, i_ + 0.72, row.res, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=4.9,
                    color=style.DEFENSE_DARK if bad else (LOOK if row.res == "TD" else style.INK_2),
                    fontweight="bold" if (bad or row.res == "TD") else "normal")
        res = RES_TXT.get(r0.fixed_drive_result, str(r0.fixed_drive_result).lower())
        ax.text(len(Dd) * CW + 0.15, i_ + 0.5, res, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=5.8,
                color=LOOK if res in ("TD", "FG") else style.INK_2, fontweight="bold" if res in ("TD", "FG") else "normal")


nd_ne, nd_sea = NE.fixed_drive.nunique(), SEA.fixed_drive.nunique()
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.5, 0.205 * (nd_ne + nd_sea + 4.2)),
                             gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[nd_ne + 1.4, nd_sea + 1.4]))
board(a1, NE, "New England offense (Seattle's defense)")
board(a2, SEA, "Seattle offense (New England's defense)")
handles = [Patch(fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec="none", label="dropback"), Patch(fc="#fbe8b8", ec="none", label="run"),
           Patch(fc="white", ec=style.INK, lw=1.0, label="successful play")]
a2.legend(handles=handles, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=3, fontsize=6.6, frameon=False)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.99, bottom=0.05, hspace=0.12)
plt.show()
```

Now read the chart the way a coach reads a tendency report: count, then ask why.

| From the chart | Super Bowl LX | 2025 regular season | League, 2025 |
|:------------------|:------:|:------:|:------:|
| New England dropbacks with four rushers | `{python} SBX["four"]` of `{python} SBX["ne_db"]` (`{python} pct(SBX["four"] / SBX["ne_db"])`) | `{python} pct(SEASON["sea_four"])` | `{python} pct(SEASON["lg_four"])` |
| Two-high coverage after the snap (of labelled dropbacks) | `{python} pct(SBX["two"])` (`{python} SBX["n_lab"]` labelled) | `{python} pct(SEASON["sea_two"])` | `{python} pct(SEASON["lg_two"])` |
| Man coverage (of dropbacks charted man or zone) | `{python} pct(SBX["man"])` | — | — |
| Pressure on New England dropbacks | `{python} pct(SBX["press"])` | `{python} pct(SEASON["sea_press"])` | `{python} pct(SEASON["lg_press"])` |
| Sacks; with four rushers | `{python} SBX["sacks"]`; `{python} SBX["sacks4"]` | — | — |
| New England snaps that were dropbacks | `{python} pct(SBX["ne_pass"])` of `{python} SBX["ne_snaps"]` | New England: `{python} pct(SBX["ne_reg_pass"])` | — |
| Seattle snaps that were runs | `{python} pct(SBX["sea_run"])` of `{python} SBX["sea_snaps"]` | Seattle: `{python} pct(SBX["sea_reg_run"])` | — |
| Kenneth Walker III | `{python} SBX["walker_n"]` carries, `{python} SBX["walker_y"]` yards | — | — |

: What the charted Super Bowl says, set against the teams' regular-season habits (Seattle's defense, unless the row says otherwise) and the league's. Two-high counts Cover 2, 2-Man, Cover 4 and Cover 6; the labelled dropbacks exclude the snaps FTN coded as COMBO. Pressure is the participation file's `was_pressure` flag on dropbacks, the same definition in every column. Source: nflverse play-by-play, FTN charting and participation; course calculation.

Four things jump out of those rows.

**Seattle did in the biggest game what it did all season, only more so.** Rushing four and playing two deep behind
it was Seattle's identity ([Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd)),
and the Super Bowl chart is that identity turned up: four rushers on
`{python} pct(SBX["four"] / SBX["ne_db"])` of dropbacks and two-high on `{python} pct(SBX["two"])` of the labelled
ones. A tendency report told New England this was coming. Knowing it and beating it are different things.

**The four-man rush didn't pressure more often; it finished.** Seattle pressured Maye on
`{python} pct(SBX["press"])` of dropbacks, no more than its regular-season rate (`{python} pct(SEASON["sea_press"])`)
or the league's (`{python} pct(SEASON["lg_press"])`). What changed was what pressure turned into:
`{python} SBX["sacks"]` sacks, `{python} SBX["sacks4"]` of them with four rushers. That's the "coverage holds, rush
wins late" bet from the strip-sack paying off across a whole game: when the coverage leaves nowhere to throw, ordinary
pressure becomes sacks. It's also the kind of claim only film can settle, snap by snap.

**The scoreboard shaped the play-calling.** New England dropped back on `{python} pct(SBX["ne_pass"])` of its snaps,
against `{python} pct(SBX["ne_reg_pass"])` in its regular season, because it trailed from the first quarter on and spent
the fourth quarter chasing three scores. Read that number as a tendency and you'd call New England's offense
pass-happy; it was a game state. Seattle, ahead all night, ran on `{python} pct(SBX["sea_run"])` of its snaps (its season
rate: `{python} pct(SBX["sea_reg_run"])`), with Kenneth Walker III carrying `{python} SBX["walker_n"]` times. The
[neutral-situation](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-neutral-situation) filter of
[Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd) exists for exactly this reason. One game's
chart describes that game, not the team.

**And the chart is silent where the film isn't.** The public rows can't tell you which of New England's two-high looks
were *shown* before the snap and which were *played* after it, which receivers Seattle's man defenders were matched on,
or who lost the block on each sack. Those are the cream-shaded columns of the sheet, and they're where the answers to
"how did Seattle do it?" live. A full chart of this game, with the film columns filled, is a weekend's project and the
best one this chapter can offer you.

### From rows to tendencies

Counting a chart is a few lines of pandas. Start from the skeleton, fill the film columns (here two of them, the
coverage and the rush, are filled from the participation file so the example runs; on your own chart you'd have typed
them), and ask the chart a question in the form *how often is it this, when it's that?*

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
from gridiron.data import nfl

# The skeleton from above, with two film columns filled from the public labels (stand-ins for your own film)
part = nfl().load_participation([2025]).to_pandas()
part = part[part.nflverse_game_id == "2025_22_SEA_NE"]
part = pd.DataFrame({"play_id": part.play_id.astype(int), "cov": part.defense_coverage_type,
                     "rush": part.number_of_pass_rushers.astype("Int64")})
chart = sheet.drop(columns=["cov", "rush"]).merge(part, on="play_id", how="left")

TWO_HIGH_CODES = {"COVER_2", "2_MAN", "COVER_4", "COVER_6"}
ONE_HIGH_CODES = {"COVER_0", "COVER_1", "COVER_3", "COVER_9"}
chart["shell_played"] = np.select([chart["cov"].isin(TWO_HIGH_CODES), chart["cov"].isin(ONE_HIGH_CODES)],
                                  ["2-hi", "1-hi"], default="?")


def tendency(chart, by, col):
    """For each value of `by`, the share of snaps with each code in `col`, and how many snaps that is."""
    t = pd.crosstab(chart[by], chart[col], normalize="index").round(2)
    t["snaps"] = chart[by].value_counts()
    return t


drops = chart[chart.play == "P"]
print("Seattle's coverage shell against New England's dropbacks, by down:")
print(tendency(drops, "down", "shell_played").to_string())
print("\nSeattle's rushers, by down:")
print(tendency(drops[drops.rush.fillna(0) > 0], "down", "rush").to_string())
```

Two lines of output and you have the start of a tendency report: what Seattle played, and how many it sent, on each
down. With your own film columns filled, the same function asks the questions no public file can.
`tendency(drops, "shell", "shell_played")` is shown against played: how often a two-high shell at the snap stayed
two-high. `tendency(chart[chart.play == "R"], "str", "dir")` is how often the runs went to the strength.
`tendency(chart, "pers", "form")` is what each personnel group lines up in. Keep the `snaps` column in view: a share
from five snaps is a hint, not a tendency, which is the same small-sample warning
[Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd) gave about the public data.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The chart is the truth about the game." A chart is a record of *one charter's judgements*, coded consistently. It's far
better than memory and far better than the box score, but its coverage column is an inference from film, its box count
depends on where you draw the box, and its "because" line is an opinion. Treat a chart the way
[Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd) taught you to treat FTN's: strong evidence
about habits across many snaps, weaker evidence about any single one.
:::

## Scoring yourself

Now the log. Since [Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)
you've been calling run or pass before the snap. Since
[How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) you've written a confidence next to each
call, and since [Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd) that confidence has been a stated number between 50% and 90%.
This section scores it.

To make that concrete, the rest of the chapter uses an example log: **every Panthers offensive snap of the 2025
season**, `{python} ME["n"]` calls across `{python} N_GAMES` games (17 regular-season games and the wild-card loss to
the Rams). The situations and the results are real. The *calls* are simulated: a reader who sees roughly what a model
using the situation and the formation sees, through some noise, and who starts the season overconfident and settles down
as it goes on.[^sim] It's a stand-in for your log, built so that its mistakes are the common ones. Its `clue` column
uses just two codes, so it can be counted: `align` on snaps where the formation moved the call away from what the
situation alone said (where the situation-and-formation model and xpass differ by more than ten points), and `sit`
where the situation alone decided it. (In [Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd) the clue column was free text;
settling on a few codes is what lets you score it.) On the website, the folded code at the top of the chapter builds
this log; `LOGDF.to_csv("prediction_log_2025.csv", index=False)` writes it out if you want to run what follows.

### Why hit rate isn't enough

The first number is the one you've been computing since Part 1: the share of calls that came true. The example reader
was right on `{python} pct(ME["acc"])` of calls. Against the bars from
[How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd), that's good: on the same Panthers
snaps, "always pass" would have been right `{python} pct(ME["always"])` of the time, the down-and-distance rule from
your first tally `{python} pct(ME["dd_acc"])`, and nflverse's situation-only xpass model
`{python} pct(ME["xpass_acc"])`.

But hit rate throws away the confidence column, and the confidence column is where most of a reader's skill shows.
Two readers can both be right 70% of the time: one who said 70% on every call and meant it, and one who said 95% on
half his calls and 55% on the rest and was wrong on a pile of the 95s. The second reader is making a mistake the hit
rate can't see. You need a score that rewards being right *and* being honest about how sure you were.

### The Brier score

That score is the [**Brier score**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-brier-score): the average, over all your calls, of
the squared gap between your stated confidence and what happened, counting what happened as 1 if the call came true and
0 if it didn't.

$$
\text{Brier} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(c_i - o_i\right)^2,
\qquad c_i = \text{stated confidence},\quad o_i = \begin{cases}1 & \text{call came true}\\ 0 & \text{it didn't}\end{cases}
$$

Lower is better. Three calls make the arithmetic plain:

| Call | Confidence | Came true? | Gap | Squared |
|:----|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|
| Pass | 0.80 | yes (1) | 0.20 | 0.04 |
| Run | 0.60 | no (0) | 0.60 | 0.36 |
| Pass | 0.90 | no (0) | 0.90 | 0.81 |
| | | | **Brier** | **(0.04 + 0.36 + 0.81) / 3 = 0.40** |

: Three calls, scored. The confident miss costs twenty times what the confident hit earned back.

Read the table as a set of incentives. A confident call that comes true costs almost nothing (0.04). A timid call that
misses costs a moderate amount (0.36). A confident call that misses costs a lot (0.81). And a reader who says 50% on
every snap, never committing to anything, scores exactly 0.25, whatever happens, because every gap is one half. So
**0.25 is the "I have nothing" line**: a log that scores worse than 0.25 has done harm by stating its confidences.

Glenn Brier, a statistician and meteorologist at the U.S. Weather Bureau, proposed the score in 1950 to grade forecasts like "70% chance
of rain", and it's still the standard way to grade probability forecasts in weather, in medicine, and in the forecasting
tournaments that taught [Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd) its habit of stating numbers.[^brier] It doesn't matter
which way round you write your calls: scoring "pass, 0.70" against whether it was a pass gives the same number as
scoring "my call, 0.70" against whether your call came true. Your log's `conf` and `hit` columns are all it needs.

### Why squared? A score you can't game

Why square the gap, rather than just averaging it, or awarding points for confidence on the calls you got right? Because
of what each rule rewards you for saying. Suppose that on a certain kind of snap, a call comes true 75% of the time, and
you know it. What should you say?

```{python}
#| label: fig-proper
#| fig-cap: "Why the Brier score squares the gap. Each curve is the score you should expect, call after call, if you always state the confidence on the horizontal axis on snaps where your call really comes true 60%, 75% or 90% of the time. Left, the Brier score (lower is better): every curve bottoms out exactly at the true rate (the dots), so the best thing you can do is say what you believe. Right, a naive rule that awards your stated confidence as points when you're right and nothing when you're wrong (higher is better): every line rises to the right edge, so it pays you to say 100% on every call, whatever you believe. A scoring rule with the Brier score's property is called proper."
cs = np.linspace(0.5, 1.0, 101)
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 2.6))
for q, col in zip((0.6, 0.75, 0.9), (style.SERIES[0], style.SERIES[1], style.SERIES[2])):
    a1.plot(cs, q * (1 - cs) ** 2 + (1 - q) * cs ** 2, color=col, lw=1.8, label=f"calls that come true {int(q * 100)}% of the time")
    a1.scatter([q], [q * (1 - q)], color=col, s=26, zorder=4, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8)
    a2.plot(cs, q * cs, color=col, lw=1.8)
a1.set_xlim(0.5, 1.0)
a1.set_ylim(0, 0.42)
a1.set_title("Brier score: say what you believe", fontsize=8.2)
a1.set_ylabel("expected score per call (lower is better)", fontsize=6.8)
a2.set_xlim(0.5, 1.0)
a2.set_ylim(0.25, 0.95)
a2.set_title("'Points for confidence': always say 100%", fontsize=8.2)
a2.set_ylabel("expected points per call (higher is better)", fontsize=6.8)
for a in (a1, a2):
    a.set_xlabel("the confidence you state", fontsize=7.0)
    a.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
    a.tick_params(labelsize=6.6)
fig.legend(*a1.get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="lower center", ncol=3, fontsize=6.6, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=2.0, rect=(0, 0.08, 1, 1))
plt.show()
```

That property has a name: the Brier score is a
[proper scoring rule](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-proper-scoring-rule). Its expected value is lowest when you
state exactly the probability you believe, so there's no way to game it by shading your numbers up or down. The
curves also explain the advice in [Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd) to rarely go above 90%: near the bottom
each curve is flat, and away from it it climbs fast. On the 75% curve, saying 80% instead of 75% costs 0.0025 a call;
saying 100% costs 0.0625, twenty-five times as much.

### Skill: compared with what?

A Brier score means little on its own; 0.19 is good or bad depending on how predictable the snaps were. So compare it
with forecasters who know less than you, on the same snaps. On the Panthers' 2025 snaps:

| Forecaster | What it knows | Brier score |
|:------------|:--------------------|:----:|
| Always 50% | Nothing | `{python} f"{REF['half']:.3f}"` |
| The base rate | The Panthers threw on `{python} pct(BASE_P)` of snaps; says that every time | `{python} f"{REF['base']:.3f}"` |
| xpass | The situation on the scorebug: down, distance, field position, score, clock | `{python} f"{REF['xpass']:.3f}"` |
| **The example reader** | What the reader saw, as logged | **`{python} f"{REF['me']:.3f}"`** |
| Situation + formation model | The situation, plus the quarterback's alignment and the number of backs | `{python} f"{REF['info']:.3f}"` |

: The example log against honest baselines, on the same Panthers snaps. xpass is nflverse's model (trained on the 2006–2019 seasons, so it has never seen these snaps either); the last row is the situation-and-formation model from Watching Live's steps 1 to 3, learned on 2024. Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play and FTN charting.

The [**Brier skill score**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-brier-skill-score) turns a comparison into one number: one minus the ratio of your score to the reference's. Against
the base rate, the example reader's skill is `{python} f"{1 - REF['me'] / REF['base']:.2f}"`, meaning the log removed
about `{python} pct(1 - REF['me'] / REF['base'])` of the error of a forecaster who only knew the team's pass rate. Against
xpass it's `{python} f"{1 - REF['me'] / REF['xpass']:.2f}"`: the reader beat "the scorebug" (xpass knows only what the
scorebug shows: down, distance, field position, score and clock), because the formation was working for him. And the
last row is the bar for a reader who uses only those two clues, the situation and the formation; the box, the shell
and the tells of [Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd) can take a reader past it. The gap between the reader and
that row is the room left with those two clues: some of it is calibration (stating the right number), some of it is the
noise of reading a broadcast in twenty seconds.

There's no published table of what a "good fan" scores, and it would mean little if there were, because the number
depends on the snaps: a team that runs on every short-yardage down is easier to read than one that doesn't. Your bars
are the baselines on your own snaps.

That's the comparison to make with your own log. **Beat 0.25** and your confidences are doing more good than harm. **Beat
the base rate** and you know more than the team's tendency. **Beat xpass** and you're reading something the scorebug
doesn't show.

### Calibration

The Brier score says *how good*. The calibration plot says *which way to adjust*.
[**Calibration**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-calibration) is how closely your stated confidences match how often
your calls come true: a well-calibrated reader's 70% calls come true about 70% of the time, his 90% calls about 90%. To
see it, group your calls by the confidence you stated, and for each group plot the stated confidence against the share
that actually came true. Perfect calibration is the diagonal.

```{python}
#| label: fig-calibration
#| fig-cap: "The calibration plot of the example log: every Panthers snap of 2025, called by a simulated reader (real snaps and results, simulated calls). Calls are grouped by the confidence stated (50–55%, 60–65%, and so on); each dot is a group's actual hit rate, plotted at its average stated confidence, with a 95% interval (the vertical bar) for how much a group of that size could wobble by chance. The diagonal is perfect calibration; below it means overconfident. Orange, games 1 to 8: from 60% up, every group comes true less often than stated, by about fifteen points in the 70s and 80s. Blue, games 9 to 18: closer to the diagonal through the middle, though still low at the top. The bars at the bottom count the calls in each group: the early reader put about half his calls at 90% or above, the later one spread them out."
def bins(conf):
    return pd.cut(conf, [0.49, 0.575, 0.675, 0.775, 0.875, 1.0], labels=False)


def wilson(k, n, z=1.96):
    if n == 0:
        return np.nan, np.nan
    p = k / n
    den = 1 + z ** 2 / n
    mid = (p + z ** 2 / (2 * n)) / den
    half = z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z ** 2 / (4 * n ** 2)) / den
    return mid - half, mid + half


def calib_table(conf, hit):
    t = pd.DataFrame({"c": conf, "h": hit, "b": bins(np.asarray(conf))})
    g = t.groupby("b").agg(n=("h", "size"), k=("h", "sum"), c=("c", "mean"), h=("h", "mean")).reset_index()
    lohi = np.array([wilson(k, n) for k, n in zip(g.k, g.n)])
    g["lo"], g["hi"] = lohi[:, 0], lohi[:, 1]
    return g


fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 4.3))
axm = fig.add_axes([0.1, 0.33, 0.62, 0.62])
axc = fig.add_axes([0.1, 0.08, 0.62, 0.17], sharex=axm)
axm.plot([0.5, 1.0], [0.5, 1.0], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
axm.text(0.955, 0.985, "perfect", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="center", rotation=36)
SERIES = [("games 1–8", FIRST, style.SERIES[1], -0.006), ("games 9–18", ~FIRST, style.SERIES[0], 0.006)]
for lab, m, col, dx in SERIES:
    g = calib_table(ME_CONF[m], HIT[m])
    axm.vlines(g.c + dx, g.lo, g.hi, color=col, lw=1.4, alpha=0.75, zorder=2)
    axm.plot(g.c + dx, g.h, color=col, lw=1.4, marker="o", ms=5.5, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=3)
    axc.bar(g.c + dx * 1.6, g.n, width=0.018, color=col, zorder=2)
axm.set_xlim(0.47, 1.0)
axm.set_ylim(0.4, 1.0)
axm.set_ylabel("how often the calls came true", fontsize=7.4)
axm.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
axm.tick_params(labelbottom=False, labelsize=6.8)
axc.set_ylabel("calls", fontsize=7.0)
axc.set_xlabel("the confidence stated", fontsize=7.4)
axc.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
axc.tick_params(labelsize=6.6)
axc.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.text(0.75, 0.9, "Games 1–8", color=style.SERIES[1], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold")
fig.text(0.75, 0.855, f"Brier {ME['b1']:.3f}\nright {pct(ME['a1'])}, said {pct(ME['c1'])}", color=style.INK, fontsize=7,
         va="top", linespacing=1.3)
fig.text(0.75, 0.72, "Games 9–18", color=style.SERIES[0], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold")
fig.text(0.75, 0.675, f"Brier {ME['b2']:.3f}\nright {pct(ME['a2'])}, said {pct(ME['c2'])}", color=style.INK,
         fontsize=7, va="top", linespacing=1.3)
fig.text(0.75, 0.52, "Below the diagonal:\noverconfident.\nAbove it:\nunderconfident.", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8,
         va="top", linespacing=1.3, style="italic")
plt.show()
```

Three things to read off a calibration plot, in this order.

**Where are the dots relative to the diagonal?** In the first half of the season the example reader's dots sit well below
it: his 70–75% calls came true `{python} pct(ME["mid1"])` of the time, and his 90%-plus calls
`{python} pct(ME["top1"])`. That's overconfidence, the commonest pattern there is: in study after study, people's
"90% sure" comes true well short of 90% of the time ([Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd) cited the classic
review). The fix is mechanical. Pull the confidences in: when you feel 90%, write 80% for a few weeks, and watch whether
the dots climb toward the line.

**How wide are the bars?** A dot from 30 calls can sit ten points off the diagonal by chance alone; a dot from 300 can't.
The vertical bars are 95% intervals for that wobble.[^wilson] Where a bar crosses the diagonal, the gap may be noise. This
is why one game can't tell you whether you're calibrated: sixty calls spread over five groups is about a dozen per group,
and every bar would span more than thirty points. A season can. As a rule of thumb, wait for about 50 calls in a group
before you trust its dot: at 50 calls, a group that comes true 75% of the time has a bar about 12 points either side.
With five groups that's roughly 300 calls, five or six games of every snap.

**How spread out are the dots?** This is the one people forget. A reader who says 60% on every snap of a team that throws
60% of the time is *perfectly* calibrated: his single dot sits right on the diagonal. He's also useless; he never tells you
anything the team's pass rate didn't. What makes a reader good is
[**resolution**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-resolution): stating different confidences on
different snaps, and having those differences come true. On a calibration plot, resolution is the dots being spread from
the bottom-left to the top-right, with the 90% calls really coming true more often than the 60% calls. The Brier score
rewards both. Calibration is knowing how sure to be; resolution is knowing more.

**A Brier score you can read off the plot.** Each dot is enough to estimate what its group costs. If a group was stated
at $c$ and came true a share $h$ of the time, each call in it costs, on average,

$$
h\,(1-c)^2 + (1-h)\,c^2 .
$$

A group stated at 90% that came true 80% of the time costs 0.8 × 0.01 + 0.2 × 0.81 = 0.17 a call; the same calls stated
at 80% would have cost 0.8 × 0.04 + 0.2 × 0.64 = 0.16. Weight each group by its number of calls (the bars under the
plot) and you have the whole log's score, near enough.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: the Brier score in three pieces"}
Allan Murphy showed in 1973 that the Brier score splits exactly into three parts:[^murphy]

$$
\text{Brier} = \underbrace{\text{reliability}}_{\text{calibration error}} \;-\; \underbrace{\text{resolution}}_{\text{knowing more}} \;+\; \underbrace{\text{uncertainty}}_{\text{the game's own}}
$$

Write each call as a chance of a pass (a "run, 70%" call is a 30% chance of a pass) and group the calls by that chance.
*Reliability* is the average squared gap between each group's stated chance and its actual pass rate: calibration error,
lower is better. *Resolution* is how far the groups' actual pass rates spread from the overall pass rate: higher is better,
and it's the only term that rewards reading. *Uncertainty* is $p(1-p)$ for the overall pass rate $p$: the part nobody can
remove, the same for every reader of the same snaps.

For the example log, games 1 to 8: reliability `{python} f"{MUR1[0]:.3f}"`, resolution `{python} f"{MUR1[1]:.3f}"`,
uncertainty `{python} f"{MUR1[2]:.3f}"`. Games 9 to 18: reliability `{python} f"{MUR2[0]:.3f}"`, resolution
`{python} f"{MUR2[1]:.3f}"`, uncertainty `{python} f"{MUR2[2]:.3f}"`. The calibration error halved: that's the
reader getting honest, and it's the cheap kind of improvement, because it takes no new knowledge. Resolution slipped a
little, partly because the later games were a different mix of snaps, which is why the total Brier score moved less than
the calibration did. Raising resolution takes reading more, which is what the rest of this course was for.
:::

### Scoring the log in Python

Here's the scoring routine. It reads a log in the final form from [Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd) (you need
at least the `call`, `conf` and `result` columns, and `clue` and `game` if you have them) and prints everything this
section has discussed. It's run here on the example log, saved as `prediction_log_2025.csv`.

```{python}
#| echo: false
_cwd, _tmp = os.getcwd(), tempfile.mkdtemp()
LOGDF.to_csv(os.path.join(_tmp, "prediction_log_2025.csv"), index=False)
os.chdir(_tmp)
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def score_log(log, base_rate=None):
    """Hit rate, Brier score, skill against the base rate, and the calibration table of a prediction log."""
    hit = (log["call"] == log["result"]).astype(float)
    conf = log["conf"].astype(float)
    brier = ((conf - hit) ** 2).mean()
    p = (log["result"] == "P").mean() if base_rate is None else base_rate
    ref = p * (1 - p)                                   # Brier score of always saying the base rate
    print(f"{len(log)} calls: right {hit.mean():.1%}, average stated {conf.mean():.1%}")
    print(f"Brier {brier:.3f} (always 50%: 0.250; base rate: {ref:.3f}); "
          f"skill vs base rate {1 - brier / ref:+.2f}")
    groups = pd.cut(conf, [0.49, 0.575, 0.675, 0.775, 0.875, 1.0],
                    labels=["50-55%", "60-65%", "70-75%", "80-85%", "90%+"])
    table = (pd.DataFrame({"stated": conf, "right": hit})
             .groupby(groups, observed=True).agg(calls=("right", "size"), stated=("stated", "mean"),
                                                 right=("right", "mean")))
    table["gap"] = table.right - table.stated           # negative = overconfident
    print(table.round(3).to_string())
    return brier


log = pd.read_csv("prediction_log_2025.csv")
score_log(log)
print("\nBy the clue you wrote down:")
log["right"] = log.call == log.result
print(log.groupby("clue").right.agg(calls="size", right="mean").round(3).to_string())
print("\nBrier by quarter of the season:")
log["part"] = pd.cut(log.game, [0, 4, 8, 13, 18], labels=["games 1-4", "5-8", "9-13", "14-18"])
log["sq_gap"] = (log.conf - log.right) ** 2
print(log.groupby("part", observed=True).sq_gap.mean().round(3).to_string())
```

And the calibration plot itself, for the whole season, in a few more lines:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| label: fig-calibration-code
#| fig-cap: "The output of calibration_plot() on the example log: the whole 2025 season in one series (the calibration plot earlier in the section splits it into two halves). Dot size is the number of calls in the group."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def calibration_plot(log, ax=None):
    """Stated confidence against the share that came true, one dot per confidence group."""
    hit = (log["call"] == log["result"]).astype(float)
    groups = pd.cut(log["conf"], [0.49, 0.575, 0.675, 0.775, 0.875, 1.0])
    t = (pd.DataFrame({"stated": log["conf"], "right": hit})
         .groupby(groups, observed=True).agg(stated=("stated", "mean"), right=("right", "mean"),
                                              calls=("right", "size")))
    ax = ax or plt.gca()
    ax.plot([0.5, 1.0], [0.5, 1.0], ls="--", color="grey", lw=1)          # perfect calibration
    ax.scatter(t.stated, t.right, s=t.calls / 3, zorder=3)                 # bigger dot = more calls
    ax.set_xlabel("stated confidence")
    ax.set_ylabel("share that came true")
    return t


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.2, 3.0))
calibration_plot(log, ax)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
os.chdir(_cwd)
```

Read the last block of the printout first. The score barely moved across the season
(`{python} f"{QTR[0]:.3f}"`, `{python} f"{QTR[1]:.3f}"`, `{python} f"{QTR[2]:.3f}"`, `{python} f"{QTR[3]:.3f}"`), and
the first four games scored as well as any stretch, though that was when the reader was at his most overconfident (he stated
`{python} pct(QTR_CONF[0])` on average and was right `{python} pct(QTR_ACC[0])` of the time). That isn't a
contradiction. A Brier score mixes how sure you were with how readable the snaps were, and the first two games were
unusually readable (they stand out in the game-by-game figure below): on snaps like those, even an overconfident
reader's 90% calls mostly come true. Week to week a Brier score measures the snaps as much as the reader; the
calibration plot, not the raw score, is what shows him improving.

The `gap` column is the calibration plot in numbers, and the clue table is the one
[How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) told you to watch: a clue you lean on
often that isn't beating the snaps where you only had the situation isn't earning its place. Careful how you read it,
though: the two rows aren't the same kind of snap. The `sit` snaps are the ones where the situation alone was lopsided,
so of course they come true more often. The fair test of a clue is against a forecaster who can't see it, on the same
snaps: on the `align` snaps the example reader was right `{python} pct(ME["align_me"])` of the time, and xpass, which
can't see the formation, `{python} pct(ME["align_x"])`. That clue is earning its place.

### Reading your report card

Once a month, or at the end of the season, run the score and match what you see to a fix:

| What the score shows | What it means | What to change |
|:-----------------------|:--------------|:-------------------------|
| Dots below the diagonal, worst at the top | Overconfident | Pull every confidence in by about ten points for a month; cap yourself at 85% |
| Dots above the diagonal | Underconfident: you know more than you admit | Push the confidences out where the formation agrees with the situation |
| Most calls between 50% and 65%, and the dots flat (each group comes true about as often as the next) | Hedging; low resolution | Use the formation step: [Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd) showed it's the one big move after the situation |
| Most calls between 50% and 65%, but the dots climb steeply and sit above the line | Underconfident, with good resolution | You're reading well; say so. Push the confidences out where the dots sit highest |
| Brier worse than the base rate | Badly overconfident, or your clues are pointing the wrong way | Check the calibration plot first; if the dots are near the line, score by clue and drop or reverse the one that's below 50% |
| Good on run/pass, poor on the second layer | Normal: coverage is hard | Keep second-layer confidences at 55–70%; check them against your chart |
| One bad game | Probably nothing | Look at the whole season; a game is too few calls to judge |

: A score is only useful if it changes what you do on the next snap.

And keep the earliest sheets. The tally from [Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)
had no confidences, so score it by hit rate only and set it against the down-and-distance rule; your first formal log
from [How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) had confidences, so give it a Brier
score too. Then put every game since on the same chart:

```{python}
#| label: fig-progress
#| fig-cap: "The example reader's season, game by game (every 2025 Panthers snap; real results, simulated calls). Top: the share of calls that came true, with the bars to beat from How to Watch a Broadcast drawn across: 'always pass' and the down-and-distance rule of your first tally, on these same snaps (the two bars nearly coincide, so they read as one line with two labels). Bottom: the Brier score per game (lower is better), with the line for saying 50% every time, the base rate, and xpass. The line is a four-game rolling average. The reader beats the scorebug (xpass) in most games, but look how far the dots jump: a game is only 43 to 76 calls, and some games are simply easier to read than others (the first two were). Week to week, the score mostly measures the games; only across a season does it measure the reader."
G = LOGDF.assign(hit=HIT, b=(ME_CONF - HIT) ** 2, xb=(CAR.xpass.values - Y) ** 2).groupby("game").agg(
    acc=("hit", "mean"), brier=("b", "mean"), xb=("xb", "mean"), n=("hit", "size"), opp=("opp", "first"),
    week=("week", "first"))
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.5, 3.9), sharex=True)
x = G.index.values
a1.plot(x, G.acc, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=0, marker="o", ms=4.2, zorder=3)
a1.plot(x, G.acc.rolling(4, min_periods=1).mean(), color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.8, zorder=2)
for val, lab, dy in ((ME["always"], "always pass", -0.017), (ME["dd_acc"], "down-and-distance rule", 0.017)):
    a1.axhline(val, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
    a1.text(18.6, val + dy, lab, fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, va="center", ha="left")
a1.set_ylabel("calls right", fontsize=7.2)
a1.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
a1.set_ylim(0.5, 0.92)
a2.plot(x, G.brier, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=0, marker="o", ms=4.2, zorder=3)
a2.plot(x, G.brier.rolling(4, min_periods=1).mean(), color=style.SERIES[1], lw=1.8, zorder=2)
for val, lab in ((REF["half"], "always 50%"), (REF["base"], "base rate"), (REF["xpass"], "xpass")):
    a2.axhline(val, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
    a2.text(18.6, val + (0.006 if lab == "always 50%" else (-0.006 if lab == "base rate" else 0)), lab, fontsize=6.4,
            color=style.INK_2, va="center", ha="left")
a2.set_ylabel("Brier score", fontsize=7.2)
a2.set_ylim(0.1, 0.28)
a2.set_xticks(x, [f"{o}" for o in G.opp], fontsize=5.8, rotation=90)
a2.set_xlabel("2025 Panthers games, in order (opponent)", fontsize=7.0)
a2.set_xlim(0.5, 18.5)
for a in (a1, a2):
    a.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=6.6)
    a.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.1, right=0.8, top=0.98, bottom=0.17, hspace=0.12)
plt.show()
```

### Scoring the second layer against your chart

Your run-or-pass calls can be scored from the play-by-play alone. The second layer can't: "zone, 65%" needs to know what
coverage was played, "five or more rushers, 60%" needs the rush count, "the run goes left" needs the direction. That's
what the chart is for. Join the log to the chart on the snap (your log has the quarter and the clock from Sunday, and
so does the chart), and score each second-layer call exactly as you scored the first: its confidence against whether it
came true.

Here it is on Super Bowl LX, with a second-layer call on every New England dropback: will Seattle play two-high or
one-high after the snap? The calls come from a scouting card, Seattle's 2025 regular-season two-high rate on dropbacks
by down, which is the kind of call a fan could make from [Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd)
before the game. The chart is the one from the tendencies section above.

```{python}
#| echo: false
_card_lit = {1: 0.63, 2: 0.48, 3: 0.44}
assert CARD == _card_lit, f"scouting-card literals out of date: {CARD}"
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
# Your live log's second layer for the game: one call per dropback, from the scouting card
# Seattle's 2025 two-high rate on dropbacks, by down (3 = third or fourth)
card = {1: 0.63, 2: 0.48, 3: 0.44}
log2 = chart.loc[chart.play == "P", ["qtr", "clock", "down"]].copy()
p_two = log2.down.clip(upper=3).map(card)
log2["l2"] = np.where(p_two >= 0.5, "2-hi", "1-hi")
log2["l2conf"] = np.maximum(p_two, 1 - p_two)                 # confidence in the call, as for the first layer

# Join on the snap, keep the snaps the chart could label, and score
scored = log2.merge(chart[["qtr", "clock", "shell_played"]], on=["qtr", "clock"])
scored = scored[scored.shell_played != "?"]                    # a "?" in the chart can't be scored
hit2 = (scored.l2 == scored.shell_played).astype(float)
brier2 = ((scored.l2conf - hit2) ** 2).mean()
two = (scored.shell_played == "2-hi").mean()
print(f"{len(scored)} coverage calls: right {hit2.mean():.0%}, average stated {scored.l2conf.mean():.0%}")
print(f"Brier {brier2:.3f}; always 50%: 0.250; "
      f"knowing in advance that two-high would come {two:.0%} of the time: {two * (1 - two):.3f}")
```

That's better than saying 50% every time, but not by much, and the reason is in the baselines. Seattle played two-high on `{python} pct(two)` of these
dropbacks, against the `{python} pct(SEASON["sea_two"])` its regular season suggested, so calls aimed at the season's
habit were aimed at the wrong number for this game: most of them said one-high on second and third down, and most of
those were wrong. One game can't tell you whether that's a flaw in the calls or a game plan built for one opponent (here,
almost certainly the game plan; the last number in the printout is a hindsight bar no one could have reached before
kickoff). Over a season you'd score second-layer calls exactly as you score the first layer, with their own calibration
plot. Expect it to be flatter, with the dots bunched between 50% and 70%: the second layer is harder, and a reader whose
coverage calls are calibrated at 60% is doing well.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: Brier score or log loss?"}
[Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd) scored xpass with *log loss*, the average of
$-\ln(\text{probability you gave to what happened})$. It's also proper, and it's what most machine-learning models are
trained on. The difference is in how it treats confident misses. A 95% call that misses costs 0.90 in Brier and 3.0 in
log loss; a 99% call that misses costs 0.98 in Brier and 4.6 in log loss; a 100% call that misses costs 1 in Brier and
infinity in log loss. For a model, that's a useful alarm. For a human log, where one careless 99% would swamp a season, the
Brier score's cap is kinder and easier to read, and it's what the best-known forecasting tournament for people, the one
behind *Superforecasting*, used.
:::

## Where to keep learning

This is the end of the course, not of the subject. Four directions are worth your time.

**The coaches themselves.** Coaches teach each other in clinics: talks at the American Football Coaches Association's
annual convention, regional clinic tours such as Glazier Clinics and the Coach of the Year Clinics (for years sponsored by Nike, so older
notes call them the Nike Coach of the Year Clinics),
and the notes and videos that circulate from them.[^clinics] A clinic talk is a coach explaining
one scheme to other coaches, with the drawings, the rules, and the problems it solves; it's the closest thing to the inside
of a meeting room a fan can get, and it's where the "why" behind most of this course came from. Read them with the
vocabulary you now have, and with the habit from [Constraint Theory and Sequencing](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd):
every scheme has a weakness the coach giving the talk is managing. Coaches have written good books, too. Bill Walsh's
*Finding the Winning Edge* is the classic on running an organisation and a game plan; for the ideas behind modern schemes,
Chris B. Brown's *The Art of Smart Football* and Tim Layden's *Blood, Sweat and Chalk*.

**The film-breakdown community.** A generation of writers and video makers now does on the internet what this chapter
asks you to do: All-22 clips, frozen frames, arrows. Ted Nguyen's All-22 breakdowns, Cody Alexander's MatchQuarters on
defense, Brett Kollmann's film-room videos, and the quarterback-focused breakdowns of JT O'Sullivan's QB School are good
places to start, and Greg Cosell's decades of All-22 study at NFL Films are behind much of the public vocabulary. Watch
how they work: freeze, rewind, one group at a time. Disagree with them when your own film says otherwise.

**The analytics community.** Everything in Part 13 came from people who publish their data and code for free. The
nflverse project (and its Python package, nflreadpy) is the foundation; Open Source Football collects worked analyses
with code; Ben Baldwin's writing explains the models behind EPA and xpass; and FTN's charting, free to use with credit
under its CC-BY-SA licence, is the public coverage and alignment data this course leaned on.

**The Big Data Bowl.** Every year since 2019 the NFL has released a slice of its player-tracking data and asked the public
to do something new with it, and its best entries have changed how the league measures the game
([Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd)). The 2026 edition
asked about player movement while the ball is in the air; as of early October 2026 the 2027 edition had not been announced,
and past editions have opened in the fall.[^bdb] If you've done the course, you can enter it: you can read a play, chart one
and model one, and the `gridiron` library you've been reading diagrams from takes Big Data Bowl tracking files directly.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: a weekly routine"}
A season-long loop that fits around a job:

- **Sunday:** the live log for one team, every snap, with a confidence (one half if that's all you can manage).
- **Monday or Tuesday:** the film for that game. Step 0 and pass 3 on every snap; the full protocol on the 20 to 30 snaps
  that decided it. Fill the chart.
- **Midweek:** score the log, update your one-page card for the team
  ([Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd)) from your chart, and pick one thing to
  watch for next Sunday.
- **Once a month:** the calibration plot, and the report card above.
- **In the off-season:** one project with tracking data, the Big Data Bowl if it's running.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: chart a full game"}
One game, one team's offense against the other's defense, end to end:

- **Before kickoff**, build the skeleton with `chart_skeleton()` from last week's game to test your setup, and write your
  codebook rules (the strength rule, where the box ends) at the top of a blank sheet.
- **During the game**, keep the live log exactly as in [Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd): every snap, the checklist,
  a call and a confidence before the snap, and a second-layer call when there's time. When the offense goes no-huddle
  and you can't get a call down before the snap, leave that row's call blank rather than fill it in afterwards: a call
  written after the snap isn't a prediction.
- **The day after**, build the real skeleton for this game, and with the coaches film run step 0 and pass 3 on every snap
  and the full four-pass protocol on third downs, red-zone snaps, sacks, turnovers and explosives. Fill every film column;
  use `?` without shame.
- **Then score it.** Run `score_log()` on the game's log for the first layer, and join the log to your chart to score the
  second layer. Write down the three snaps that cost you the most Brier score, and the "because" line for each.
- **Keep the files.** One game is a start. A season of them is a calibration plot, a chart of a team, and the best
  football education you can give yourself.
:::

## Predict the play

These drills are the film room's version of the course's habit: predict first, then check. The first two are pre-snap
frames from the film, and the question is what the next pass of the protocol will show. The third is a scoring drill.

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: pass 3, before you press play"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-rotation
#| fig-cap: "Frozen at the snap. Second-and-8 at midfield, ball on the offense's left hash, so the wide side of the field is to the right. Shotgun, 11 personnel, two receivers each side. The defense is in nickel with two safeties deep (both lettered S here, since which one is 'free' or 'strong' is what the drill asks), but not evenly: the safety on the short side (left, ringed) is at about 9 yards and pinched toward the ball, while the field safety (right) is at 14 yards, just outside the far hash. Both corners are about seven yards off with outside leverage, and the nickel ($) is splitting the difference between the slot and the tackle on the field side."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
DMV = {"FS": (9.0, -3.2), "SS": (14.0, 8.0), "LCB": (7.0, -15.6), "RCB": (7.0, 15.6), "NB": (5.0, 6.2),
       "MIKE": (4.5, 1.6), "WILL": (4.5, -2.4)}
dfn = [p_.moved(d=DMV[p_.key][0], w=DMV[p_.key][1]) if p_.key in DMV else p_ for p_ in dfn]
dfn = [p_.moved(label="CB") if p_.pos == "CB" else p_.moved(label="S") if p_.pos in ("FS", "SS") else p_
       for p_ in dfn]
pr1 = Play(off, dfn, los=60, to_go=8, ball_y="left")
pr1.highlight("FS")
fld = pr1.draw(lateral=(-20, 23), window=(-8.5, 19.0), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
scorebug(fld, pr1, ["Q2  7:40", "2nd & 8, 50"], at=(-6.6, -18.3))
tag(fld, pr1, "boundary safety: 9 yd, pinched", (11.4, -10.4), fs=6.4)
tag(fld, pr1, "field safety: 14 yd, wider", (16.6, 11.5), fs=6.4)
tag(fld, pr1, "field →", (-6.8, 19.6), fs=6.4, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()
```

**What coverage will pass 3 show after the snap, how sure are you, and what will you watch first to find out?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Single-high after the snap, about 60–65%, most likely Cover 3 with the boundary safety rotating down; watch the
*field* safety's first step.** The shell is two-high, but it isn't a balanced two-high: one safety is four yards shallower
than the other and pinched toward the ball. That's the tell from the tells catalogue in
[Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd): when two safeties disagree, the shallower, narrower one is usually the rotator.
He's already close enough to drop into a short zone on the boundary side at the snap (a
[buzz rotation](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-buzz-rotation) if he goes to the hook area, a
[sky rotation](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sky-rotation) if he goes to the flat), and the field safety, already wide,
would then run to the deep middle. Look at the slot on the short side, too: nobody is aligned over H. The pinched
safety is the only defender who can get to that area quickly, another sign that he's the one coming down. The corners
fit: off, outside leverage, eyes inside is the alignment of a corner who will bail to a deep third and keep everything in
front of him and outside him ([The Cover 3 Family](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd)), and the seven-yard
cushion is the zone-ish part of that clue.

Why not 90%? Because disguise is the norm ([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)):
the pinched safety could be a quarters safety cheating to take away a slot route, or bait for a quarterback who reads
exactly this tell. The field safety's width argues the other way: he's well outside the middle of the field, and to
become the single-high safety he has to cover a lot of ground at the snap. And Cover 1 is possible too, with the same
rotation: the pinched safety comes down as the [robber](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-robber) in the short middle
and the corners turn and run with their receivers instead of bailing.

What to watch: the **field safety's first step**. If he drives toward the middle of the field, the middle is closing and
it's single-high. If he backpedals straight, it's still two-high, and the pinched safety was playing a quarter or a half
from a cheated spot. Then the corners: bail (Cover 3) or turn and trail (Cover 1). On the chart: `shell 2`, then `cov C3`,
`rot B` if you were right (`B*` if the safety held his spot until the snap and only then came down).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: pass 1, a guard on his heels"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-power
#| fig-cap: "Frozen at the snap. Second-and-4 at the opponent's 45, first quarter. 21 personnel in an I-formation: the quarterback under center, the fullback (F) and tailback (T) behind him, the tight end (Y) on the right. The defense is in base, a 4-3 with the Sam linebacker (S) walked up onto the line outside the tight end, one safety deep (FS) and the strong safety (SS) walked down outside the Sam: eight in the box. Defensive tackles are lettered T too; the tailback is the T in the offense's backfield. On the end-zone angle, the left guard (arrow) is set a little deeper than the center and the right guard, with less weight on his hand. The drawing exaggerates his depth so it shows: in reality it's a matter of inches, and he must still be on the line of scrimmage."
off = offense("i_form")
off = [p_.moved(d=-1.45) if p_.key == "LG" else p_ for p_ in off]
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off)
dfn = [p_.moved(d=5.5, w=8.6) if p_.key == "SS" else p_.moved(d=1.0, w=6.0) if p_.key == "SAM" else p_
       for p_ in dfn]
dfn = [p_.moved(label="CB") if p_.pos == "CB" else p_ for p_ in dfn]
pr2 = Play(off, dfn, los=75, to_go=4)
fld = pr2.draw(lateral=(-20, 20), window=(-9.5, 16.0), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
scorebug(fld, pr2, ["Q1  9:15", "2nd & 4, opp 45"], at=(-7.4, -18.4))
tx_, ty_ = fld.xy(*pr2.to_abs(-5.0, -8.0))
gx_, gy_ = fld.xy(*pr2.to_abs(-1.45, -1.6))
fld.ax.annotate("", xy=(float(gx_), float(gy_)), xytext=(float(tx_), float(ty_)), zorder=20,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.INK, lw=1.0, shrinkA=12, shrinkB=5))
tag(fld, pr2, "left guard: deeper,\nlight hand", (-5.0, -8.0), fs=6.3)
tag(fld, pr2, "8 in the box", (8.6, 3.0), fs=6.6)
plt.show()
```

**What will pass 1 show at the snap, which way will the run go, and which defender will nobody block?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A gap run to the right, most likely power: the left guard pulls, the line blocks down, and two defenders go
unblocked: the backside end by design and the walked-down safety by arithmetic. Run about 75%; right, about 65%.** Start with run or pass: second-and-4 from 21 personnel under center is a run look,
though eight in the box is the defense inviting play-action, so not 90%.

The guard is the scheme tell from [Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd)'s catalogue: a lineman about to pull sideways
sets up for it, with less weight forward and a little depth. A pulling left guard runs to the right, toward the tight end,
so this looks like **power** ([Gap and Power Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd)). What pass 1 should
show, if that's right, against this front: the center blocks *back* on the tackle shaded toward the pulling guard's
side; the right guard and right tackle double-team the tackle outside the guard and one of them climbs to the backside
linebacker; the tight end blocks down on the end over him; the fullback runs at the Sam, the last man on the line, and
[kicks him out](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-kick-out); and the left guard pulls behind the line and turns up through
the hole the kick-out and the down blocks create, looking for the middle linebacker.

**Who's unblocked?** Count it. Power brings seven blockers to this front (the five linemen, the tight end and the
fullback). The left tackle spends his on the gap the guard left, so six of them block a defender, and eight
defenders are in the box: two are free.
One is the defensive end on the *left*, the backside, left alone on purpose: he's too far from the play to matter if
it's fast enough. That's the trade power makes: it spends the backside guard to get an extra blocker at the point of
attack, and it accepts one free defender chasing from behind. The other is the strong safety, walked down outside the
Sam. Nobody has him; he's the defense's extra man, and the back has to make him miss. That's why runs into eight-man
boxes are so often checked to play-action, or sent with a receiver cracking down on the safety. If the film shows the
backside end making the tackle, the "because" line is about speed (the play was too slow, or the back hesitated); if
the safety makes it two yards downfield, the call lost to the eight-man box.

And if the line instead steps *together*, all to one side, with no puller, the guard's stance was a false tell: it's zone,
and you note it in your clue column.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: two readers, one season"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-readers
#| fig-cap: "Two readers' calibration plots for the same season of snaps (every 2025 Panthers snap; real results, simulated calls). Both called run or pass on every snap and got almost exactly the same share right. Reader A (orange) stated 90% or more on most calls. Reader B (blue) never went above 85%, and most of his calls were 50–65%. The bars at the bottom count each reader's calls at each confidence level."
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
axm = fig.add_axes([0.1, 0.36, 0.6, 0.6])
axc = fig.add_axes([0.1, 0.1, 0.6, 0.17], sharex=axm)
axm.plot([0.5, 1.0], [0.5, 1.0], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
for lab, conf, hit, col, dx in (("A", A_CONF, HIT_A, style.SERIES[1], -0.006), ("B", B_CONF, HIT_B, style.SERIES[0], 0.006)):
    g = calib_table(conf, hit)
    g = g[g.n >= 10]
    axm.vlines(g.c + dx, g.lo, g.hi, color=col, lw=1.4, alpha=0.75, zorder=2)
    axm.plot(g.c + dx, g.h, color=col, lw=1.4, marker="o", ms=5.5, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=3)
    axc.bar(g.c + dx * 1.6, g.n, width=0.018, color=col, zorder=2)
axm.set_xlim(0.47, 1.0)
axm.set_ylim(0.4, 1.02)
axm.set_ylabel("how often the calls came true", fontsize=7.4)
axm.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
axm.tick_params(labelbottom=False, labelsize=6.8)
axc.set_ylabel("calls", fontsize=7.0)
axc.set_xlabel("the confidence stated", fontsize=7.4)
axc.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
axc.tick_params(labelsize=6.6)
axc.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.text(0.74, 0.88, "Reader A", color=style.SERIES[1], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold")
fig.text(0.74, 0.83, f"right {pct(AB['a_acc'])}\naverage stated {pct(AB['a_conf'])}", fontsize=7, color=style.INK,
         va="top", linespacing=1.3)
fig.text(0.74, 0.68, "Reader B", color=style.SERIES[0], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold")
fig.text(0.74, 0.63, f"right {pct(AB['b_acc'])}\naverage stated {pct(AB['b_conf'])}", fontsize=7, color=style.INK,
         va="top", linespacing=1.3)
plt.show()
```

**Which reader has the better Brier score? What's each one's mistake, and what should each change?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Reader B scores better (`{python} f"{AB['b_b']:.3f}"` against `{python} f"{AB['a_b']:.3f}"`), though both are making
a fixable mistake in opposite directions.** Both were right on about `{python} pct((AB['a_acc'] + AB['b_acc']) / 2)` of
calls, so the whole difference is in the confidence column.

**Reader A is overconfident.** His dots sit below the diagonal all the way up, and his 90%-plus calls, the bulk of his
log, came true only `{python} pct(AB['a_90'][0])` of the time. Each of those misses costs between 0.8 and 1 in Brier score.
With the back-of-envelope rule from the calibration section: that group, `{python} pct(AB['a90_share'])` of his calls,
was stated at `{python} pct(AB['a90_c'])` on average and came true `{python} pct(AB['a_90'][0])` of the time, so it cost
about `{python} f"{AB['a90_cost']:.2f}"` a call; stated at its true rate it would have cost
`{python} f"{AB['a90_fixcost']:.2f}"`. B's big group, the `{python} pct(AB['b_lo_share'])` of his calls at 65% or less,
was stated at `{python} pct(AB['b_lo_c'])` and came true `{python} pct(AB['b_lo_h'])`: about
`{python} f"{AB['b_lo_cost']:.2f}"` a call. The comparison is closer than the pictures suggest, which is why the
answer has to come from the numbers rather than the look of the plot. The fix for A: pull everything in. His calls already sort snaps well (his dots climb from left to right, which is resolution);
his numbers are just too big.

**Reader B is underconfident.** His dots sit *above* the diagonal: his 70% calls came true far more often than 70%. He knows
more than he admits, and he never stated more than `{python} pct(AB['b_top'])` on any snap. The fix: push the confidences
out where the clues agree, toward 90% on the empty-backfield, third-and-long snaps.

How much is at stake? If each reader replaced every stated confidence with the rate at which those calls actually came
true (perfect calibration, the same calls), A's Brier score would fall to `{python} f"{AB['a_fix']:.3f}"` and B's to
`{python} f"{AB['b_fix']:.3f}"`. Same reading, better numbers. That is the cheapest improvement in the whole course, and
the calibration plot is how you find it.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Film answers what Sunday can't.** The All-22 shows all 22 players for the whole play; the coaches film's end-zone angle
  shows the line. Use them to check your reads, not to rewrite them.
- **Four passes, in order.** Freeze at the snap and grade your read; then the line, the quarterback, the coverage, the skill
  players, from what sets the clock to what uses it; then one "because" line that says whose play it was.
- **A chart turns a game into rows.** Same fields, same codes, every snap, with `?` allowed. Let the play-by-play fill a
  third of it; the film columns are where your chart knows more than any public file.
- **Score with a proper rule.** The Brier score rewards being right and being honest about how sure you were; 0.25 is "I
  have nothing", and the base rate and xpass are the bars to beat.
- **Calibration is how sure; resolution is how much.** Read the calibration plot for which way to adjust, the spread of the
  dots for whether you're learning anything, and never judge either from one game.

- The nflverse data dictionaries (play-by-play, participation, FTN charting) and Open Source Football: the columns behind
  your skeleton, and worked analyses to copy.
- The NFL's Big Data Bowl page at operations.nfl.com and the competition pages on Kaggle: past winners' notebooks are a free
  course in tracking data.
:::

[^gorilla]: Daniel J. Simons and Christopher F. Chabris, "Gorillas in our midst: sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events," *Perception* 28 (1999): 1059–1074. In the best-known condition, about half of the observers counting passes failed to notice the person in the gorilla suit.

[^nflplus]: The history and the current package are covered, with sources, in [How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd): Buffalo Bills, "Watch film like a coach with Game Rewind" (July 30, 2012), https://www.buffalobills.com/news/watch-film-like-a-coach-with-game-rewind-7721721 ; NFL.com, "Launch of NFL Pro highlights third season of NFL+" (2024), https://www.nfl.com/news/launch-of-nfl-pro-highlights-third-season-of-nfl . Timing: NFL+ Help Center, "How do I watch Coaches Film" (All-22 "available 24-36 hours after the completion of each game"), https://support.nfl.com/hc/en-us/articles/35869780989332-How-do-I-watch-Coaches-Film .

[^lx]: Score, date and site: nflverse schedules and play-by-play (game `2025_22_SEA_NE`); "Super Bowl LX," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LX . Quarter-by-quarter, Seattle led 3–0, 9–0 and 12–0 at the ends of the first three quarters, all on Jason Myers field goals.

[^ssfacts]: nflverse play-by-play, FTN charting and participation for game `2025_22_SEA_NE`, the Patriots' third-quarter play with 0:16 left: "D.Maye sacked at NE 37 for -7 yards (58-D.Hall). FUMBLES (58-D.Hall) … RECOVERED by SEA-91-B.Murphy at NE 37." Personnel, alignment, motion, box, rushers and the coverage label (`2_MAN`) are FTN's charting, not the teams' calls. The touchdown that followed: "S.Darnold pass deep right to 88-A.Barner for 16 yards, TOUCHDOWN," 13:29 of the fourth quarter.

[^timing]: Release timing from the nflverse data dictionaries and update workflows. In season, nflverse rebuilds play-by-play after each game window (Thursday night, Sunday early and late, Sunday and Monday night) and again every morning (https://github.com/nflverse/nflverse-pbp/blob/master/.github/workflows/update_data.yaml); it checks FTN for new charting every six hours (https://github.com/nflverse/nflverse-ftn/tree/main/.github/workflows); and participation (personnel and coverage), supplied by FTN, is released only after the season ends. Dictionaries: https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_ftn_charting.html , https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_participation.html .

[^kappa]: Jacob Cohen, "A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales," *Educational and Psychological Measurement* 20 (1960): 37–46. Kappa compares the agreement you observed with the agreement two coders would reach by chance, given how often each uses each code.

[^lx2]: Seattle's and New England's 2025 coordinators as listed for Super Bowl LX: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LX and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Seattle_Seahawks_season (Kubiak offensive coordinator, Durde defensive coordinator).

[^sbdata]: nflverse play-by-play, FTN charting (via `load_ftn_charting`) and participation (via `load_participation`) for game `2025_22_SEA_NE`; plays with `play_type` pass or run and a down recorded, so two-point tries, kneels, spikes and penalties that wiped out a snap are not on the board. Coverage labels and rusher counts are FTN's charting; FTN's data is used under the CC-BY-SA 4.0 licence. Success is nflverse's `success` flag (EPA greater than zero).

[^sim]: The example log uses every Panthers run and dropback of the 2025 season with an xpass value (nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting), including the wild-card game. For each snap, a "situation + formation" model (a logistic regression on nflverse's xpass, the quarterback's alignment and the number of backs, learned on the 2024 regular season) gives the chance of a pass; the simulated reader sees that chance on the log-odds scale multiplied by an overconfidence factor (1.5 in the first game, falling to 0.95 by the last) plus random noise, calls whichever side is more likely, and rounds his confidence to the nearest 5%, capped at 95% in the first eight games and 90% after. Results are the real plays. The readers in the third drill use the same method with fixed factors (A: 2.2, B: 0.35). The xpass baseline is nflverse's model as shipped, trained on the 2006–2019 seasons (`seasons <- 2006:2019` in https://github.com/nflverse/nflfastR-data/blob/master/models/_dropback_model_data.R ).

[^brier]: Glenn W. Brier, "Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability," *Monthly Weather Review* 78, no. 1 (1950): 1–3. Brier's original version summed over both outcomes, so it runs from 0 to 2; the version used here (and almost everywhere today) is half of that for a yes-or-no event, running from 0 to 1. Brier worked in the Weather Bureau's Office of Meteorological Research from 1939: "Glenn W. Brier," Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_W._Brier .

[^wilson]: The intervals are Wilson score intervals: Edwin B. Wilson, "Probable inference, the law of succession, and statistical inference," *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 22 (1927): 209–212. They behave better than the simple "plus or minus two standard errors" when a group is small or its hit rate is near 100%.

[^murphy]: Allan H. Murphy, "A new vector partition of the probability score," *Journal of Applied Meteorology* 12 (1973): 595–600. The split is exact when calls are grouped by their distinct stated values, as here (confidences rounded to 5%).

[^bdb]: NFL Football Operations, "Big Data Bowl": https://operations.nfl.com/gameday/analytics/big-data-bowl . The 2026 edition (the eighth) studied player movement while the ball was in the air, using 2023-season tracking data; no 2027 edition had been announced as of October 6, 2026.

[^clinics]: AFCA, "AFCA Announces General Speakers for the 2026 AFCA Convention" (Charlotte, January 11–13, 2026), https://www.afca.com/afca-announces-general-speakers-for-the-2026-afca-convention/ ; Glazier Clinics' 2026 calendar (27 football clinics, January to March), https://glazierclinics.com/clinics ; Coaches Insider lists 2026 Coach of the Year Clinics (Orlando, Tunica, Atlanta) after Nike-branded series through 2024, https://coachesinsider.com/football-plus/ .

[^gjp]: In the Good Judgment Project, the team Tetlock led in the forecasting tournament run by IARPA (the U.S. intelligence community's research agency) from 2011, every forecaster was scored with the Brier score; Tetlock and Gardner, *Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction* (Crown, 2015), ch. 3.

[^nws]: Nate Silver, *The Signal and the Noise* (Penguin, 2012), ch. 4, on the calibration of U.S. National Weather Service precipitation forecasts. The original evidence: Allan H. Murphy and Robert L. Winkler, "Reliability of subjective probability forecasts of precipitation and temperature," *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C (Applied Statistics)* 26 (1977): 41–47.
